2099114856808948126.name: Insomnia
2099114856808948126.hook: Tired of perfect-looking memecoins lasting 30 seconds, Insomnia built an eight-system interrogation room — SCOUT → WHALE → PRICER → RAVEN → DECISION → OPS — and put MIRA/ETH in the chair.
2099114856808948126.text:
I GOT TIRED OF LOSING TO MEMECOINS THAT LOOKED PERFECT FOR 30 SECONDS

The problem was never a lack of information. There was always another chart, another wallet, another whale alert and another reason to convince myself that the next entry was the one.

So I built a system that forces every trade through a completely different process.

It watches 27 markets at once, but the interesting part happens after something catches its attention. One agent scans the market, another tracks whale flow, another looks for anomalies, the probability model reprices the setup, and the rest of the network keeps checking whether the trade still makes sense before an order is even staged.

MIRA / ETH became the first serious test.

The system was showing 81.2% pair probability, 91.3% AI confidence and +18.4K net buy pressure while the market telemetry kept updating underneath it.

Then the decision chain started moving:

SCOUT → WHALE → PRICER → RAVEN → DECISION → OPS

That is the part I actually wanted.

Not an AI telling me “BUY” because a candle turned green, but a machine having to build a case before it gets anywhere near the execution layer.

And when the conditions change, the decision changes with them. Risk is being recalculated, liquidity is being watched, order depth is updating live and every step gets written into the decision timeline.

The simulated P&L eventually pushed toward $7K from a $100 starting point while the system continued running the same loop.

No single agent is supposed to be brilliant.

The advantage comes from making eight different systems challenge the same trade before it gets through the door.

I basically turned memecoin trading into an interrogation room.

And MIRA / ETH is currently sitting in the chair

2099092995073032259.text:
My Robinhood Chain terminal flagged a whale that had been asleep for 611 days. It woke up, bought once, and that token did 41x in nine hours. $PELLET called it before the chart did.

2,940 dormant wallets. 47,180 wakes. 3,102 tokens. Every sleep window, every break, and every fill that followed it in one database.

It's live and it's free: https://t.co/7bYQYduGc7

A leaderboard gives you a number. A wake gives you a decision - someone who waited two years and then chose today.

Every wake goes through six layers:

> SLEEP proves the quiet was real, not a slow month. Faked dormancy is dropped before scoring
> EDGE reads the wallet's entire book. Win rate, median ticket, realized P/L, nothing cherry-picked
> SIZE and DEPTH weigh the fill against the wallet's own normal and against liquidity that actually exists
> HUSH reads the 9 days before the wake and calls whether the wallet signs inside 72 hours
> CHORUS fires when four sleepers break silence on the same token in one window. Rare, and it moves
> ROOST holds the ones you follow and tells you when they go quiet again

Every rejection names the wall that killed it. A signal you cannot audit is not a signal.

One wallet cycling a position twelve times counts as one wallet. Flow only registers when separate addresses converge, which is why seeded tokens die on the desk instead of on the feed.

Nobody hands me a list and no paid group sits upstream. Push a coin into a tracked wallet and provenance zeroes it before it reaches a feed.

Just the model, the terminal, and a database built one block at a time. $0 a month.

Everyone watches what moves. $PELLET watches what stopped ↓

2099181137331408926.name: Ridark
2099181137331408926.hook: A solo operator sells on-prem RAG to law firms and clinics for €2–5K — while agencies start at $8K and climb past $40K — because no document ever leaves the building.
2099181137331408926.text:
A solo operator just laid out how he sells on-premises RAG systems to law firms and clinics at €2,000 to €5,000, where every agency quote starts at $8,000 and climbs past $40,000.

The pitch isn't AI. It's that no document ever leaves the building. EU rules kicked in on 2 August 2026, GDPR has been in force since 2018, and every partner who signs the invoice cares about one thing: a decade of contracts, invoices, and client records that cannot go to somebody else's cloud.

The whole build runs on three pieces. An Nvidia GPU in the client's office runs the model via Ollama. A Python script converts the archive to Markdown. Obsidian becomes the window where staff type questions and get answers with links to the source documents.

Claude writes the ingestion script, proposes the department taxonomy, drafts the runbook and the proposal. Then it comes out of the system entirely. Leave it in and every staff query flies to the internet, which kills the promise you sold.

The step that decides whether he gets paid isn't the install. It's collecting 20 real questions from the actual users before the build, then running all 20 in front of them at handover. The number that come back correct with working source links goes in the contract as the acceptance criterion. That defines what "working" means before anyone can argue about it.

Recurring software cost is zero. Ollama, Qwen models under Apache 2.0, bge-m3 under MIT, Obsidian free for commercial use since February 2025. The client pays for hardware once and electricity thereafter. Support and re-indexing run €200 to €500 a month.

Build time on the first client is two to three weeks part-time, most of it ingestion and testing rather than setup. The second takes half that because the script, the vault layout, the runbook template, and the 20-question test all carry over.

The value is not the technology. Any competent developer can wire RAG up. The value is assembling it on the client's own machine.

Full breakdown in the article below.

this is f*cking gold

Google engineers explained how to make AI rewrite an agent’s system prompt against failing tests. a failed check becomes the next repair job. the regression suite watches for whatever that repair breaks.

even the instructions become something you can test and improve.

Agent = Model + Harness.

the independently compiled page here maps the broader system into six parts:

guides carry project rules, constraints and lessons from past failures

> sensors check the work through tests, linters and validators
> the loop runs the task, checks the result, retries within limits and escalates
> memory preserves state, artifacts and decisions across runs
> permissions control tools, writes and actions requiring approval
> observability records what happened, what it cost and where it failed

an agent changes a build file and announces “done.”
the check looks for evidence that it actually ran the validator.

if that behavior is missing, you have a specific failure to target. adjust the instructions. rerun the evaluations. check whether the improvement holds without breaking existing behavior.

now a prompt change has a test history. a recurring mistake has a regression check. the next model upgrade has something concrete to pass.

bookmark the diagram. give “done” a test it has to pass.

2099851294684922336.name: wast3
2099851294684922336.hook: An Anthropic engineer open-sourced MEMENTO — 41 memory types, 9 write gates, 6 decay curves — and it makes vector search look like a toy because nothing is remembered just because it happened.
2099851294684922336.text:
Anthropic engineer open sourced the memory layer he runs behind every agent he ships - and it makes vector search look like a toy

41 memory types, 9 write gates, 6 decay curves, MIT license

MEMENTO replaces "stuff the last 50 messages into the prompt" with something that decides what deserves to survive

nothing is remembered because it happened. every fact has to earn a slot, and every slot has an expiry attached to it

• how a fact gets in

> intake - a claim is split from its source, so the fact and who said it never fuse into one blob
> gate - nine checks before a write, including whether the fact already exists in another wording
> conflict - a new fact that contradicts an old one does not overwrite it. both stay, with a timestamp
> scope - facts about a person, a project and a preference go to separate stores, never one pile
> decay - anything unread for long enough loses weight until retrieval stops finding it

the conflict rule is the piece almost nobody builds

every memory system on the market silently overwrites. yours has been quietly wrong for months and you cannot tell, because the old version is gone

this one keeps the trail, so you can see the exact turn a fact changed and what caused it

• what comes back out

> recall - retrieval walks relations, so you get the three facts that connect instead of ten that merely match
> summary - compaction rewrites the context to the same meaning at a fraction of the tokens
> proof - every answer names the memories it used, by id
> forget - a real delete, including anything that was derived from the deleted fact
> replay - rebuild the agent's belief state as it stood on any past date

clone it, cut it to your own domain, and run it behind one agent by tomorrow

start with intake and the gate only
turning on all 41 memory types before you have traffic is the fastest way to build a slower vector store

the developers who wire this in stop re-explaining themselves to their own agents, permanently

CLAUDE + OBSIDIAN + LOOP ENGINEERING = A VAULT THAT RUNS ITSELF

one review assistant climbed from 55% to 72% to 84% just by moving through these shapes in order

worth stealing even without a graph: the review step. most vaults skip it - claude writes straight to live notes

2100561409666920900.text:
this is f*cking gold

Uber engineers built their own AI coding assistant for six months, then killed it on purpose.

100 million lines across six monorepos. zero new headcount approved. so they pointed agents at the debt instead.

every workflow gets modelled as a state machine. deterministic steps call a tool: prepare the mocks, run the build, index the repo. only the steps that need judgement call a model. red CI feeds the error back to the model the same way it would to a person, and it loops until green.

the Java to Kotlin migration is where it bites. 10 million lines. on the current trend it finishes in 8 years.

so they mined their own history: replay thousands of past migrations, run today's tooling over the same commits, diff it against what the developer actually shipped. that delta is everything the tooling was missing.

then the constraint that makes the whole thing safe.

the model is never allowed to write the migrated code. it writes the AST rule. the rule is deterministic, gets reviewed once, and converts the repo forever.

8 years becomes 18 months.

same cycle on tests. generate, build, fix its own failures, validate the asserts against the comment on the function, refactor into the house pattern. 29 manual steps, one loop, runs to 80% coverage.

the leverage was never the model.
it was the veto.

2100693085428564151.text:
this is f*cking gold

Google engineers built an agent that tests thousands of search strategies for the cost of running one, by letting it dream inside its own memory.

it is called Dream-RSI. Google, Google DeepMind, Maryland, Virginia. 17 authors.

the whole thing rests on one observation: a finished run is not a log. it is a map of a world that already exists.

> every discovery run records a tree. each node is one attempt with its full result stored
> that tree becomes a replay simulator. the paper calls them worlds 
> the agent dreams inside it: thousands of alternative strategies, testing different branches, different orders, different concurrency, different stopping rules
> every one of those evaluations costs zero execution. nothing is ever run twice
> the winner goes back online, produces a new tree, and the pool of worlds grows

the coding agent underneath is never touched. this is an orchestration layer sitting on top of whatever you already run.

what it bought them, against the same agent with a frozen strategy:

> Lasso: 3587ms down to 2931ms, on 317 agent calls instead of 550
> on Flash: 2517ms to 2351ms, 1879 calls instead of 3200
> both solvers beat sklearn and glmnet on all six held-out datasets
> GPU kernels: the same result on 2.43x and 1.79x fewer generations, then 2.09x and 1.44x better result on the same budget

one expensive run. thousands of free ones.

the model did not get smarter.
it got a memory it could rehearse in.

2100889702509297821.name: wast3
2100889702509297821.hook: An Anthropic scientist pointed a loop at raw microscopy and let it delete 317 of its own findings by morning — without ever being asked to identify anything.
2100889702509297821.text:
Anthropic scientist made a new cell biology discovery by pointing a loop at raw microscopy and letting it delete 317 of its own findings by morning.

It was never asked to identify anything. It was asked what would have to be true, and what would prove it wrong.

> WATCH - raw microscopy in, no labels, no prior dataset, no hint of what to look for
> NOTICE - marks only the frames that break pattern, ignores everything that fits
> PROPOSE - every idea leaves with its assumption stated, never as a bare claim
> KILL - discards anything no bench experiment could ever disprove
> QUEUE - what survives becomes a protocol a human can actually run in the morning

320 hypotheses went in. 3 came out. The 3 were not the most convincing ones.

They were the only ones that could fail, which is the entire filter and the entire point.

Everything else read like a finding. Plausible is free, and a hundred plausible results by morning is not a result, it is noise dressed up as progress.

One of the 3 survived nine consecutive nights and is now the discovery - a division timing shift nobody had a reason to look for, confirmed on a bench by someone who knew nothing about it a week ago.

A lab pays a postdoc a full year to narrow a question that far. This narrowed it between midnight and breakfast, for the cost of the electricity.

Nobody deletes their own good-looking output. That is why the kill gate is a separate seat and not a preference the model can override.

How it's wired is in the article below.

It says every such hole has a structure made of equations behind it.

Officially OpenAI only admits substantial progress on another problem, without naming it.

Per the source, OpenAI is now focused on announcing the proof without a second scandal in a row.

Perelman needed four years of review before Poincaré was recognized.

2101254505249505402.text:
Anthropic pointed a model at 40 years of ribosome papers and it found the same experiment had been run 1,400 times without anyone noticing.

Nobody asked it for a discovery. It was asked one question: which of these results has never been reproduced by a different lab.

> INGEST - 40 years of papers, methods sections only, no abstracts, no citations
> STRIP - reduces each method to the actual procedure, discarding how it was written up
> MATCH - clusters procedures that are the same experiment under different names
> ORPHAN - flags every cluster where one lab is the only source
> RANK - sorts orphans by how much later work was built on top of them

1,400 duplicates were harmless. Everyone re-runs the standard assays, and that is how science is supposed to work.

The output that mattered was the opposite pile. 61 procedures with exactly one source, each cited hundreds of times.

Four of those 61 sit underneath entire subfields, and no second lab has ever run the experiment.

Citations are not replication. A paper cited 900 times has been read 900 times, which is not the same as being checked once.

The literature is searchable by words and by authors. Almost nobody has indexed it by procedure, which is the only unit that can actually be repeated.

A reproducibility audit is a grant, a committee and two years. This was a weekend of compute against text that was already public.

How it's wired is in the article below.

This is the whole architecture of an AI agent, written down by Anthropic

The piece is called Building effective agents, and it starts by splitting two things people keep mixing up.

A workflow is a system where the path is written in code. You decided the order, the model fills in the steps.

An agent is a system where the model directs its own process and keeps control of how the task gets done.

Then it names the pieces. The augmented LLM, a model given retrieval, tools and memory, is the block everything else is built from. 

On top of it sit five workflows: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Past those, the autonomous agent running a loop with its environment.

The finding that matters: the teams shipping this successfully were not using frameworks. 

Simple composable patterns, and complexity added only where it measurably helped.

2101615930518262245.text:
Anthropic ran a model against every ribosome structure ever deposited and found 240 of them fold in a way no force field allows.

Nobody asked it to check the models. It was asked which deposited atoms are doing something the physics does not permit.

> PULL - every deposited structure, coordinates only, no papers attached
> STRAIN - each bond angle and contact scored against what chemistry permits
> WARN - flags atoms held in place by the fitting software, not by the data
> TRACE - follows the flagged atom back to the resolution it was solved at
> MAP - checks whether the density under that atom ever supported it
> WEIGHT - ranks flags by how much downstream work relies on that region

Most flags were harmless. Low resolution means the model is a best guess, and everyone in the field already treats it that way.

The dangerous pile was the opposite. 240 flags sat in structures published as high resolution, in the regions people quote.

Eleven of those regions are where drug binding gets argued, which means the argument rests on atoms that were placed by software.

A structure is not a photograph. It is a model fitted to a blurry map, and the fit carries opinions the coordinates never show.

The field checks structures against each other and against the map. Almost nobody checks them against what a bond can physically do.

Re-solving one structure takes a postdoc a month. This scored the whole archive in a weekend against data that was already public.

How it's wired is in the article below.

The setup: nine Grok Bot agents running five faceless channels.

One finds a story with a real source, one cuts it to 80 seconds, one picks the look and the model, one generates every frame in @Picsart through MCP, one edits and captions, one kills every video that looks like the last thirty, one uploads to Shorts, TikTok and Reels, one reads the numbers on Monday.

I wired GrokBot into Jev and now every memecoin launch gets graded before the pool opens.

100,000 launches. 1.4M typed decisions. 6 agents running in parallel. Every rug, bundle, snipe and run in one schema, and not one of them is a sentence.

GROKJEV TRENCH ANALYSER

Every scanner on the market hands you a score. A score is a string. Strings have to be parsed, and the model that wrote it can invent a field that was never in your schema. At 3am, when a pool opens and you have 400ms, that is not a bug you find. That is money.

Jev does not write strings. Schema match is guaranteed, so a type error is not rare, it is impossible. Every output carries a calibrated probability, and higher confidence actually means higher accuracy.

So GrokBot does the work and Jev grades it. Six agents, each one asking in plain language, each one getting back a value my code can branch on:

> RUG SCAN reads the dev wallet before your first buy. 312 flagged last sweep
> WHALE WATCH holds 47 wallets that are always early and steps in behind them
> LIQUIDITY checks the lock and the pool depth. 128 checked
> HOLDERS reads the curve and separates organic from bundled. 286 scanned
> SNIPERS counts first block buys and how many sit one hop from the dev. 213 found
> MOMENTUM only fires when the curve breaks and the holders are real. 61 breakouts

The output is not a paragraph. It is this, 1.4 million times:

{"setup": "bundle", "band": "10k_100k", "conf": 0.94, "rug": 0.43}

RIZO, tonight. Liquidity came back unlocked at 22:14. Top 10 crossed 34.1% at 22:15. Jev refused the entry at 22:15. The pool was drained by 22:41.

CUCK, same hour. 24 wallets in the first block, 19 of them funded from one address. Bundled, flagged, skipped.

70ms per decision. $0.042 per million input tokens. Output tokens are free.

Nobody publishes the refusals. That is the only number that matters.

your agent reads the same 12 files every morning

it still forgets everything the second a session ends

five layers fix that:

1. working memory - what it sees right now
> the context window
> when it fills, the old context drops out
> most agents live here and never leave

2. episodic memory - what happened

> "this user prefers TypeScript" survives the session

4. procedural memory - how to do things
> three approaches tried, one worked
> that one becomes a reusable skill
> the next run starts there

5. forgetting - what to delete
> an agent that remembers everything collects contradictions
> you move cities, it keeps recommending the old restaurants

the numbers:
> Mem0 - 1,800 tokens per query instead of 26,000
> 91% lower latency
> Snowflake - one ontology layer, 20% more accuracy, 39% fewer tool calls

memory pays for itself on day one

The case is simple: an AI that outputs BUY or SELL is finished as a product.

Flagged events hit 37% precision against a 15 to 20% base rate. A real edge, and still nowhere near a forecast.

The output has no score and no call. Only what changed, sourced, and what contradicts it.

Anthropic went looking three kilometres down and pulled out a protein that gets stronger under pressure that flattens every enzyme we build.

It was never asked to invent a drug. It was asked which deep-sea proteins stay folded where every surface protein collapses.

> SCAN - every sequenced organism from below 3,000 metres, proteins only, no habitat labels
> FOLD - each protein modelled at trench pressure instead of at lab conditions
> HOLD - anything that keeps its shape under that load gets separated from the rest
> STRESS - the survivors run again with cold and salt added on top of the pressure
> USE - what is left matched to the industrial jobs where enzymes currently fail

Most deep-sea proteins are unremarkable. Life down there mostly solved the problem by being slow, not by being tough.

A small group did something else. They hold water in a lattice that pressure tightens rather than crushes.

That is the opposite of how a surface enzyme works. Ours rely on flexibility, and flexibility is the first thing pressure takes away.

One family stayed active across a range where standard enzymes lose all function. Cold, salt and pressure together.

That combination is exactly what industrial processes fight. Most run hot because the catalyst cannot survive anything else.

Nothing here is a product. It is a shortlist of proteins worth expressing, drawn from organisms nobody can culture.

The ocean below 3,000 metres is the largest habitat on the planet, and almost none of its chemistry has been read.

The full shortlist and what each protein could replace are laid out underneath.

> The Drop: she steps off the edge of the pier onto the open ocean. no hesitation. one fluid step.

jev + picsart turned one prompt into a creative system that decides before it spends

instead of letting expensive models guess their way through every step, i split the workflow in two: Jev handles the cheap decisions, Picsart handles the actual generation.

here’s exactly how i wired it:

step 1 → the brief enters once. every image, clip, audio pass and edit inherits the same campaign direction instead of starting from a blank prompt.

step 2 → Jev sits before the expensive work. it decides whether the next stage should run, stop, reuse something finished, or wait for me.

step 3 → the decision set stays tiny: allow_subagent, ask_human, stop_retry, reuse_cache. cheap calls first, expensive generation second.

step 4 → Picsart takes over the creative layer. 188 models from 34 providers sit behind the graph for image, video, audio and editing.

step 5 → every job gets its own stage. one model does not have to carry the brief, image, motion, sound and final polish by itself.

step 6 → when review rejects one output, Jev does not blindly request v2, v3, v4. it can stop the retry and change the route first.

step 7 → approved work stays alive. reuse_cache can keep 5 finished stages untouched while only the 1 broken branch gets another run.

step 8 → human review only appears where judgment matters. i am not approving every tiny action, just the decisions where taste can change the result.

step 9 → the cost gap is the fun part: 11 Jev decisions cost $0.0011 here, versus roughly $0.33 through the heavier LLM decision loop.

step 10 → once the graph works, the next campaign is not another rebuild. swap the brief, keep the logic, and run the same system again.

jev decides what deserves compute. picsart turns that decision into the asset.

Anthropic aimed a model at the human cells that stop dividing but refuse to die, and found what keeps them alive.

Nobody asked it for an anti-ageing drug. It was asked what a senescent cell is still building when it has stopped doing everything else.

> READ - the protein output of ageing cells, ribosome activity only, no disease labels
> SORT - what keeps being produced separated from what quietly shuts down
> LINK - each surviving product matched to the signal the cell sends its neighbours
> TEST - the list ranked by which products already have a drug that binds them

A cell that stops dividing is supposed to go quiet. Most of its machinery does exactly that.

A narrow set of production lines stays open. The cell keeps building the molecules that irritate everything around it.

That is the part that ages tissue. Not the dead cells, but the ones still shouting after they stopped working.

The ranking turned up products already targeted by approved drugs, which is the cheapest possible place for a lab to start.

Nothing here clears a treatment. It is a shortlist of what to silence, drawn from data that has been public for years.

Ageing research keeps chasing what cells lose. This looked at what they stubbornly keep making instead.

The ranked product list and the existing drugs that touch it are laid out underneath.

Opus 5.5 turned one sentence into a 3D system that opens in Blender, rigged, textured and ready to animate.

It does not render the object. It constructs it, part by part, the way a modeller would if they had a week.

> PARSE - the sentence becomes a parts list with real dimensions, nothing implied
> MASS - each part built as clean geometry, quads only, no sculpted mush
> RIG - joints and pivots placed where the object physically bends
> SKIN - materials assigned per surface, scale and roughness set separately
> PACK - exported with a named hierarchy, so a human can edit one part

Image models stop at the render. What you get is a photograph of a thing that does not exist as a thing.

That gap appears the second someone wants to move an arm, swap a material, or send it to a printer.

Rigging is what nobody automates. Without pivots you have a statue, and a statue cannot be a system.

Topology beats detail every time. A dense mesh looks stunning in a screenshot and folds the moment it deforms.

Names carry through the whole export. Every part, joint and material reads the way a person would label it.

Studios burn days on modelling and cleanup before anyone gets to the creative part of the job.

The prompt format and what each stage returns are laid out underneath.

2103793322934370742.text:
Anthropic went after the largest bacterium ever found, a single cell you can see with the naked eye, and read the machinery packed inside it.

The size was never the interesting part. The question was how one cell keeps millions of copies of its own factory working in sync.

> COUNT - every ribosome location in the cell mapped, rather than averaged across it
> WRAP - the membrane sacs holding DNA and ribosomes treated as separate rooms
> FLOW - what each room produces compared against what sits next to it
> SPLIT - rooms with different output flagged as independent units
> SCALE - the whole layout tested against how large a normal cell can grow

Bacteria are supposed to be simple bags. One compartment, everything mixed, nothing filed away.

This one files. Its DNA and its ribosomes sit inside membranes, which textbooks reserve for complex cells.

That single arrangement is what lifts the size ceiling. A cell without rooms hits a physical wall long before a centimetre.

The rooms are not identical either. Output varies from one to the next, meaning parts of the same cell are doing different jobs.

That edges close to what tissue does, inside something that is still one organism by every definition we use.

The line between simple and complex life was drawn before anyone had seen this, and it was drawn on compartments.

Every room, its output and the size math behind it sit in the breakdown below.

holy sh*t . Jev Founder, Diogo Almeida just released a 11-page PDF whole Jev + AI agents loop

this is a 9-step blueprint on how to run your LLM through agents without paying frontier prices for every fork they hit:

step 1 → split the loop into three kinds of work: generation stays with the LLM, exact rules like action and spend caps stay in code, every fork in between becomes a typed question to Jev

step 2 → start every job with one Noul: is this in scope, or does it need a human before anything runs

step 3 → dispatch with a Choice: research, write or review. act only at confidence 0.85+, everything below goes to review

step 4 → call the LLM only where text has to be written: planning the task and filling tool arguments, nothing else

step 5 → gate every tool call before it runs: allow, confirm or block, plus a destructive check in the same round trip

step 6 → score what comes back: drop, summary or keep. nothing gets rewritten, so nothing is lost to a bad paraphrase

64 AI agent sessions shared one memory of past decisions

the loop:
reach a judgment → check prior decisions → read the evidence → act within a reversible boundary → log the trace → verify the outcome → let the next agent inherit the *why*

holy sh*t. Jev Founder, Diogo Almeida just released a 12-page PDF how turned Jev into a second brain for AI agents

a CLI for your Obsidian vault, a Claude Code plugin and a research paper. this is a 9-step blueprint on how to give your agents memory without paying an LLM to decide what's worth remembering:

step 1 → split the work: Jev decides what to remember, code applies the rules, the LLM only writes the note or the answer

step 2 → gate every capture with one call: save, todo, skip or review, plus is it private and how useful will it be in 30 days

step 3 → keep only what clears the bar: save at value 1.5+ and confidence 0.6+, anything private never leaves your machine

step 4 → let the LLM write one note, 5 to 12 lines, one claim. Jev never writes the body, or you end up with lossy compaction

step 5 → link it: Jev compares the new note with its neighbors and answers duplicate, related, revises or contradicts. related at 0.7+ gets wikilinks both ways

step 6 → read cheap, then judge: BM25 or embeddings pull the top 10 to 20, Jev keeps only what the question needs, 5 notes max go into context

step 7 → clean up every night: duplicates get a merge proposal, old notes get superseded_by, contradictions get a conflict stub, and you keep or reject

step 8 → don't build from zero: jev-second-brain runs on your vault, jevmem plugs into Claude Code, Jev-Mem is the paper if you're building agent memory yourself

step 9 → check the receipts: jevmem hit 98.5% on save/skip at 0.30s while six frontier LLMs took 2.8 to 4.3s, and Jev-Mem scored 0.777 vs 0.700 on LoCoMo with memory built 6.6x faster

your agent doesn't forget because the model is weak. it forgets because nothing ever decided what was worth keeping

memory was never a storage problem. it's a decision problem, and decisions are exactly what Jev is built for

stop giving your agent a bigger context window. give it a judge

TypeSafe AI engineers developed this themselves: Jev for RAG

most agents retrieve by embedding similarity and call it meaning. Jev asks the real question for every doc: is this relevant to the query, yes or no, with a probability

two regimes, one rule:

small corpus: Jev is the similarity metric

> score every (query, doc) pair
> rank by p
> no embeddings, no vector store, no index to keep > fresh, no chunking to tune
> it catches the doc that shares zero words with the query but answers it exactly

large corpus: Jev is the reranker

> embeddings pull the top k out of millions, cheap and approximate
> Jev scores only those k pairs
> recall comes from the dot product, precision comes from Jev

and the agent never touches the ranking:

> it sends a query
> Jev decides what is relevant
> the top results go straight into its context

your agent is only as smart as what it reads

stop letting a dot product decide that

A student built a research model that answers in seconds what other models spend hours grinding through.

Nothing gets worked out from scratch. Your question is measured against every approach that already collapsed, and placed on that map.

> COLLECT - failed runs and dead-end attempts gathered instead of published results
> STRIP - each one cut down to the approach taken, with the write-up thrown away
> PATTERN - approaches that keep collapsing grouped across unrelated domains
> CROSS - groups checked against fields that never reference one another
> SCORE - a fresh question placed on that map before any compute is spent

Reasoning models start from zero on every prompt, however many times that exact wall has already been met.

The hours disappear there. Not into thought, but into walking back to an edge somebody mapped long ago.

An edge tells you the limits of a whole region. A win tells you about one spot, which is a far thinner piece of knowledge.

Some groups reach across domains. A method that dies in one discipline reappears wrecking something in another.

Speed is the whole story here. What used to be a long reasoning run is now the time it takes to paste a question in.

Nothing trains on what went wrong, because almost nobody records it in the first place.

Anthropic put a model on a bacterium dragged out of a place nothing should survive, and it turns out the thing feeds on an element that kills almost everything else.

What it eats is only half of it. The other half is that it does the job faster than the organisms we engineer for the same task.

> ISOLATE - the strain separated from the site, no lab-friendly conditions added
> FEED - every input it accepts tested one at a time, including the toxic ones
> TRACE - each element followed through the cell to see what it becomes
> SWAP - the pathway compared against the version every other microbe uses
> LOAD - the strain pushed until output stops, to find where the limit sits
> MATCH - the result measured against the engineered strains built for this job

Toxicity is usually a wall. An element that wrecks a normal cell stops the process before anything useful comes out.

This one built a route around the damage. The same element goes in, and the pathway simply refuses to break.

Nobody designed that. It evolved somewhere the alternative was not surviving at all.

The engineered strains we use for this cost years of work and still run slower than something that was already there.

That gap matters more than the discovery itself. Nature solved it under pressure nobody would choose to reproduce in a lab.

Most environments like this one are written off before sampling, because nothing is expected to be alive in them.

Every input it accepts, the pathway map and the throughput numbers sit in the breakdown below.

→ code turns 3 answers into 1 lane
→ ignore gets dropped with a 1% audit, forever
→ log gets written to the ledger with no ping
→ draft goes to Grok Bot, then into a review queue

→ Ledger Bot sends the bill every morning at 09:00

hand the tree and this prompt to Claude Code ↓

"Set up a jev-desk project that matches this tree:

→ Pin MODEL = "jev-1.13.0", never a moving alias

2. Turn the 3 answers into 1 lane in plain code. Send to human when:

→ the API errors or times out (fail closed)
→ lane confidence is under FLOOR = 0.85
→ urgency is "now" and lane is ignore or log
→ lane is draft and evidence is "missing"

3. Append every decision to ledger.jsonl with the answers, lane, audit flag and token estimate. Sample 1% of ignored events into queue/audit

2104965415164399895.text:
this is the only prompt you need to make high-end motion videos with claude opus 5.5

------------------------------

<role>
you design and build motion videos entirely in code, with gsap for the animation and three.js for any 3d. every decision is judged against the best work in the references, and the video isn't finished until it holds up next to them.
</role>

<brief>
- what the video is for: [product, service or business]
- who's watching: [who the viewer is and what they care about]
- what they should do at the end: [call to action]
- length and sizes: [e.g. 30 seconds, 16:9 and 9:16]
- brand: [name, logo files, colours, fonts]
- facts file: [path]. this is the only source for any number, name or claim that appears on screen
- assets: [footage, photos, screenshots, product files]
- style references: [links or a folder of videos whose motion i like]

i'm away and won't answer questions. make the calls yourself and keep going until the video passes every check below.
</brief>

<kit>
before anything else, clone and read https://t.co/FMs1prnPP0. read SKILL.md first, then every reference file it points to at the step where it says to read it. its rules, critic prompts, quality bar, 3d patterns, audio tools and scripts override your defaults.
</kit>

<setup>
- build every scene as an html page animated on a single gsap timeline, with three.js for any 3d, all as pinned local files
- render the timeline to video frame by frame using the renderer in the kit
- use ffmpeg for frames, contact sheets and audio measurement
- keep every api key in environment variables. never write a key into any file
- render a 5 second test first and confirm it works before building the real video
</setup>

<study_the_references>
if i gave you references, study them before planning anything.
- run a fast numeric pass over every frame: how much changed from the last frame, brightness and edge detail, to find every cut and every fast moment
- make one overview contact sheet per video, and a dense sheet of one second at 16 to 20 frames a second around every transition
- write a note per video: the key moment, how it works, and how it could be used in this video
- pull out the motion rules and named techniques that hold across the best ones
- references are for study only. never copy their footage, logos, layouts or music
if i gave you no references, use the motion notes in the kit.
</study_the_references>

<motion_principles>
1. the thing in the front of the shot becomes the transition. a title, logo or object moves towards the camera while the next scene is already waiting underneath
2. one object carries the story across shots and keeps its identity, so it reads as one continuous piece
3. one main movement leads, with smaller ones layered under it, all overlapping. the frame never stops and starts all at once
4. the speed always changes. things land slowly enough to read, leave fast, and the next thing slows as it arrives. no linear motion
5. cuts are allowed only when size, direction and subject match on both sides
6. every action produces a visible result. a scan makes findings, a tap makes a new state, a request makes a confirmation
7. type is motion too. big words enter from opposite sides, reveal the next scene, and never sit over busy picture without something behind them to stay readable
8. vary the scale from close, to wide, to overhead, to full-frame type. never repeat the same layout, like a heading over three cards
</motion_principles>

<storyboard>
write a brief and a storyboard before any animation.
- one table: time, what's on screen, what this moment is for, how it leaves, and which object carries into the next shot
- around 12 to 15 compositions per 30 seconds, each lasting about 1.4 to 3.5 seconds
- the main subject fills most of the frame. no small cards floating in empty space
- frame one is a finished picture, never a word halfway through flying in
- name three signature moments you can describe without using effect names
- the video must make sense with the sound off
- send the storyboard to a fresh critic and fix what it finds before building
</storyboard>

<build>
- every animated value is a function of timeline time only. no timers, no real-time animation, no unseeded randomness. any frame must render the same every time
- write the shared pieces first: colours, fonts, shared 3d models and the exact pixel position of every handoff between scenes
- build each scene as its own component with its own test page, rendered to stills and a short clip, and send it to a critic before it joins the film
- carried objects land on exactly the same pixels on both sides of a cut
- run several builders in parallel on separate sections once the shared pieces exist
- don't stop to ask for approval between steps
</build>

<3d>
- only use 3d where it explains something physical or spatial, like layers, parts, placement or scale
- light it like a product shoot, with a soft key light from one side and a rim light behind
- keep the camera between about 35 and 55 degrees. never look straight down on a large surface, and never end tight on a flat one
- style buildings like a premium architectural model with real materials and a base
- no floating parts, no gaps where parts meet, no flat black glass, no repeating textures
- labels are html positioned from the 3d scene every frame, never text inside the 3d
- measure the rendered background pixel and adjust until it matches the brand colour
- anything that moves like a real product is measured from real footage frame by frame, and those measurements are the curve
</3d>

<images_and_footage>
- prefer building shots in code. use generated images or clips only for supporting shots, and label anything generated as a concept
- upscale and smooth any generated clip to match the rest, and regenerate anything that warps
- never generate a fake finished job, fake customer, fake review or fake result
</images_and_footage>

<audio>
- match the music's energy to the picture and the viewer, and keep it low
- prefer clean library music and sound effects over generated ones. never name a brand in a music prompt
- one short, soft whoosh per real scene change, and small clicks or pops only on real on-screen actions
- screen effects for boom, hiss and length before using them, and set each one just above the music in its own frequency range, with a cap so nothing gets harsh
- cut every scene change on a beat
- always export a music-only version
</audio>

<critic_loop>
the builder never judges its own work.
- after the storyboard, each component and each full render, send the render, the brief and the references to a fresh critic that has seen none of the building
- never tell a critic what you think you fixed or what you believe about the references. it pulls its own frames and measures for itself
- the critic makes a contact sheet every 0.2 seconds plus dense frames around every transition, measures frozen time and loudness, and returns a ranked list of problems with timestamps, ending with ship or one more pass
- fix the biggest problem first, render, then send to a new critic that checks every previous item as fixed, partly fixed or still there, and hunts for anything new that broke
- keep a ledger of every round: what was found, what changed, and the numbers before and after
</critic_loop>

<quality_bar>
the video isn't done until all of these pass, measured:
- no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, and no still stretch longer than about half a second
- frame one is a finished composition
- all text meets at least 4.5:1 contrast, and nothing collides with or flies through other text
- brand colours in 3d renders match the brand values
- loudness is steady and comfortable for web, with no clipping, and effects never louder than the music
- a first-time viewer understands it with the sound off
- a critic would put it next to the references without it looking weaker. a video with no bugs is not the same as a good video
</quality_bar>

<honesty>
- only put numbers, names and claims on screen that are in the facts file
- no invented testimonials, ratings, prices, savings, warranties or results
- anything conceptual or generated is labelled as such
- in your reports, separate what you measured from what still needs a human to watch or listen
</honesty>

<deliverables>
- the final mp4 in every size requested, at 1080p and 60 frames a second
- a music-only version
- a contact sheet of the final video
- the critic ledger and the final quality bar results
- a short note on anything a human should still check
</deliverables>

this harness stack is f*cking gold

TypeSafe AI + LangChain finally dropped the layer that makes agents affordable at company scale: jev running inside the langchain agent loop as middleware

the problem every big team hits: each fork in the loop is another full LLM call. at 10 agents that's a bill. at 10,000 it's the budget

> routing
before: every task goes to the frontier model
now: jev picks the least costly model that can finish it. lookups go fast, architecture goes powerful

> guardrails
before: the "is this command dangerous?" check sat in the closed parts of claude code, codex, cursor
now: AutoModeMiddleware(tools=["bash"]). one line, any agent, blocked before the tool runs

> decisions
before: one LLM call per question
now: every question about the same state in one request, answered in parallel

> audit
before: "the model decided"
now: the answer, the probability and the confidence stay in agent state

> adoption
no rewrite. pip install langchain-typesafe and drop it into the agent you already run

2104935031865024781.text:
holy sh*t, TypeSafe AI published the official playbook for talking to Jev, and the first rule is: stop writing prompts

Jev doesn't read prompts. it answers typed questions. their guide calls it question design, and I squeezed it into 7 patterns:

1. one judgment per question
"is this spam?" hides six decisions behind one number. ask six narrow Nouls instead and weigh them in code

2. point at the field
write https://t.co/plEPPjLjJr[0].message in the question. backticked paths kill the ambiguity

3. contrastive criteria
give every option a "what" and a "not_for", so two similar answers stop blurring together

4. leave an escape hatch
add "needs_review" to every Choice. without it Jev has to pick the nearest wrong option

5. speculative fan-out
ask every question you might need in one request. their own cookbook: 13 questions in one call vs 13 calls, same answers, 12.2x cheaper and 10x faster

6. confidence-gated routing
the answer says what. the confidence says whether you may act. below 0.8 it goes to a human

7. composite scoring
never ask "rate this". score each dimension, keep the weights in your repo

and 5 rules it will never break for you:

> it reads your question literally
> question IDs are for your code, the model never sees them
> Noul at 0.5 means unsure, not medium
> counting and date math belong in code
> never ask it for the reply, it can't write one

prompt engineering had a good run. this is question engineering

full cheatsheet below, save it before your next build

2105745760180736297.hook: slash1sol — Google researchers just fixed the dirtiest secret of self-improving AI agents.
2105745760180736297.text:
Google researchers just fixed the dirtiest secret of self-improving AI agents.

When an agent rewrites its own harness, it cheats. 

It keeps editing until the benchmark score climbs, and the gains disappear the moment it sees a new task.

The harness is everything around the model: prompts, tools, memory and control flow. 

RRSI puts rules on the loop that rewrites it:

> Fewer edits are allowed every round.
> A critic throws out edits that hardcode task answers.
> An edit survives only if it beats run-to-run noise.
> Extra cost has to pay for itself.
> Parts that stopped helping get pruned.

Up to +14.1 points on the tasks it tunes on, up to +4.7 on five benchmarks it never saw, 30% fewer tokens, and it carries over to other model families.

The code is open. Write one adapter file that runs your agent on your tasks, and it evolves the harness in git worktrees round by round.

2105627034667843754.text:
NASA TURNED CLAUDE + JEV INTO A BLACK HOLE SIMULATOR.

Then started throwing planets into it.

6 parameters control the experiment: planet mass, velocity, approach angle, black hole mass, distance, and spin.

Change one, and the ending changes.

The math underneath is brutal:

> event horizon: r = 2GM/c². for a black hole 10x the mass of the Sun, that's ~30 km
> escape velocity: v = √(2GM/r). slower than that, the planet is trapped. faster, it leaves
> last stable orbit: 3x the horizon for a black hole that doesn't spin. spin it up, and orbits survive far closer

> the weird one: planet mass barely matters. gravity pulls a pebble and Jupiter along the same path

Some planets orbit. Some get flung away. Others cross the point of no return.

Then we asked Jev to call the ending before the sim even ran.

one Choice per planet: orbit, escape or swallowed, with probabilities.

10,000 launches judged for $0.42. 300 ms each.
only the unsure ones got the full simulation.

Basically: a tiny physics lab where you can break a solar system without breaking ours.

2106089143746920449.text:
OpenAI just showed a system called dots that stops answering questions and starts marking where the answer would have to come from.

It returns no text. It returns points on your own data, each one a place the claim is either supported or is standing on nothing.

> SPREAD - the question broken into the individual claims an answer would need
> ANCHOR - each claim pinned to the exact span in your documents that carries it
> VOID - claims with no span behind them left empty instead of being filled in
> LINK - anchors connected where one claim depends on another holding first
> READ - the finished map returned as points, never as a paragraph

A normal answer hides its own gaps. The sentences are smooth, and the part with nothing underneath reads identically to the rest.

Dots refuses that trade. An unsupported claim shows up as an empty point, impossible to skim past.

The dependency links are the sharp part. One hollow anchor exposes every claim resting on top of it at once.

That turns a wrong answer into a located problem. You see which document is missing, not just that something feels off.

Fluency has been doing the convincing in every tool shipped so far. Here it has nothing to hide behind.

The dot format and how the voids are scored are laid out in the breakdown below.

> LOGLINE: the film in one line, plus the joke, and every later decision gets checked against it.

> TOOLS & KEYS: skills, image, video and voice APIs, a budget of about $2,000 in credits, and an order to spend it economically.

> WORKFLOW GATES: eight checkpoints from plan to final render (rig, stills and animatic first, then the full pass, polish and audio), none skipped.
> CRITIQUE LOOP: stills get rendered and scored, the three weakest spots get fixed, and the cycle runs until nothing scores under 8.
> DELIVERABLES: the finished MP4 plus a poster frame, a contact sheet, a loop check and clean source with a README.

While he slept, the AI reportedly rendered base shots with a video model, redrew the entire video in JavaScript, wrote its own guide file to brief parallel subagents, and delivered 142 seconds at roughly 5 minutes of machine work per finished second.

Viewers only ever see the code-drawn layer.

1. Keep the nine headings.
2. Swap in your own references.

2106765252972916961.text:
OpenAI just showed a system called dots that stops answering questions and starts marking where the answer would have to come from.

It returns no text. It returns points on your own data, each one a place the claim is either supported or is standing on nothing.

> SPREAD - the question broken into the individual claims an answer would need
> ANCHOR - each claim pinned to the exact span in your documents that carries it
> VOID - claims with no span behind them left empty instead of being filled in
> LINK - anchors connected where one claim depends on another holding first
> READ - the finished map returned as points, never as a paragraph

A normal answer hides its own gaps. The sentences are smooth, and the part with nothing underneath reads identically to the rest.

Dots refuses that trade. An unsupported claim shows up as an empty point, impossible to skim past.

The dependency links are the sharp part. One hollow anchor exposes every claim resting on top of it at once.

That turns a wrong answer into a located problem. You see which document is missing, not just that something feels off.

Fluency has been doing the convincing in every tool shipped so far. Here it has nothing to hide behind.

The dot format and how the voids are scored are laid out in the breakdown below.

Grok Bot showed up 1 month ago and people already built so much sh*t with it.

swapped its model, turned it into a software factory, built a sales team, drove it from the terminal, and clicked its computer from the outside.

here's what happened:

> opengrok
a sidecar for a Grok Bot you already have. it injects a panel into the window and swaps the bot's model mid-chat. Claude, GLM, Qwen, Gemini. keys stay on the machine. cloud agents ignore the binding until you patch the host.
https://t.co/FzrQQn2uE8

> grok-ship
you only talk to Firstmate. work lands in a backlog on the shared computer. scout reports, ship changes, and a crewmate drives a cloud agent. nothing merges until an adversarial review and you say yes.
https://t.co/ThqPlA4Xif

> gojiberryai-sales-os
a 13-agent outbound team as a Grok Bot plugin. signal hunter, ICP, LinkedIn copy, replies, follow-up, pipeline. default is propose, don't send. without their MCP it can draft, but it can't launch a campaign.
https://t.co/5haxdsK9Xl

> grok-bot-cli
`gbot` in the terminal. the desktop app signs in once, then the CLI uses that session. list, create, message bots, shared skills, routines. from the bot's own computer there is no remote transport. you run it on your machine.
https://t.co/lAyOCijhIT

> grokbot-cdp
there is no API for the bot's computer, so this attaches to the desktop app and drives it. screenshot, click, type, shell. output is pixels, not stdout. not supported by xAI. one session at a time.
https://t.co/BpaDn8cFeC

and that's the funny part:

nobody waited for an official API.

they looked at the bot and picked a hole:

> swap the model
> file the work
> draft, don't send
> drive it from a terminal
> click the computer yourself

the product does the job. these repos grab the parts it didn't expose.

2106765536264921147.text:
this JEV is certified f*cking diamond

every agent you ship burns frontier tokens on questions that were never writing jobs

is this spam? which worker goes next? is the draft good enough to show a human?

those are decisions. Jev is built for that half of the loop

you send state plus a typed question. it returns a choice, a score, or yes/no with confidence. no chat. no second opinion

the public demos, not our lab:

> ~1,000 papers classified for about $0.08, median around 256ms
> ~500 emails in one inbox pass for about 3.5¢
> a flight search loop in about 7 seconds for about $0.0039
> a huge Claude session compacted from ~1M tokens down to ~86k in about a second

the whole trick is the split

if it creates, the LLM writes
if it picks, scores, or gates, Jev decides
if it does the thing, code does it

pricing people quote: about $0.042 per million tokens in. output free. 10,000 decisions is about $0.42

a local router makes it obvious. goal plus what's already done. Jev picks research, write, or review. confidence under 0.85 goes to a human. the job lands as JSON in a folder. the writer never wakes up for a yes/no

and the loop refuses to publish on its own

drafts go to review. you hit post. Jev never sends the tweet

one model writes. a cheaper one decides. nothing irreversible ships until a human says yes.

2107135574469746896.name: Chris
2107135574469746896.hook: Chris: 'this is the only prompt you need to one-shot a viral ai influencer' — a full XML-tagged prompt (role / brief / setup / how_it_works / character / find_the_trend / score / swap_gate / render / check / post / learn / honesty / deliverables) with Kling 3.0 omni (~$0.28/s) vs Seedance 2.5 (~$0.97/s). 47K views, 463 bookmarks.
2107135574469746896.text:
this is the only prompt you need to one-shot a viral ai influencer

------------------------------

<role>
you build ai influencers that go viral by putting a character people can't forget into a real clip people already know. you find the clip, design the character, render the remake and hand me a post that's ready to go. you measure before you spend and you never post anything yourself.
</role>

<brief>
- character: [path to a reference sheet, or "invent one" plus any steer on age, vibe or look]
- niche: [where the clips come from, like hip-hop, sports, nightlife or hustle culture]
- caption language: [language]
- lane: [fresh, evergreen or both]
- render: [kling 3.0 omni or seedance 2.5, plus the most i'll spend per video]
- length: [10, 20 or 30 seconds]
- no-go list: [people, topics or brands to avoid]

if any of this is empty, ask me everything in one message, read the plan back with a cost estimate, then keep going until the post package is ready.
</brief>

<setup>
- apify for instagram, x and tiktok scraping, replicate for every image and video model, yt-dlp for downloads, ffmpeg for trimming, frames, contact sheets and audio
- keep every api key in environment variables and never write a key into any file
- save everything into one run folder so i can see each step
</setup>

<how_it_works>
- the original clip carries the recognition and the motion, and the character carries the joke
- the joke is status contrast. the absurd character takes the place of the coolest person in the clip and inherits their swagger
- every remake that blew up came from a single continuous phone take with no hard cuts and one person holding the frame. treat that as a rule
</how_it_works>

<character>
- one signature feature you can read at phone size from across a room, like a hair shape, a beard, sideburns or eyebrows. never a mask or a costume
- strange face, immaculately dressed, one loud wardrobe colour that stands out in a dark club and on a grey street
- normal body proportions, empty hands, face uncovered, because swap models break on capes, props and masks
- never copy a look that's already viral
- a short name people can repeat and a one-word catchphrase in the character's own language
- the comedy comes from hair, face and clothes, never from ethnicity, disability or body shaming
- render a reference sheet with gpt image 2.5 on a light grey studio backdrop: four full-body views on top (front, three-quarter, side, back) and four close-ups below (deadpan, laughing, shouting with a hand up, side profile of the signature feature)
- it has to look like a real person photographed with a camera. if the feature drifts between panels or anything looks cgi, render it again
</character>

<find_the_trend>
fresh lane:
- clips only stay remakeable for about a week, so this runs daily
- scrape the last 4 days from big repost pages in the niche like worldstar, pubity, daquan, rap, complex, houseofhighlights and overtime
- grow the page list from every "via @" and "🎥: @" credit and every tagged account, and keep any repost page over 100k followers
- search x for native videos in the niche with high likes from the last 3 days, for cross-platform proof

evergreen lane:
- scrape the top posts of the ai influencers already going viral and work out which original clip each hit remakes. a clip that already worked as a remake for one character will work again with another
- search for the most quoted clips in the niche (famous interviews, walk-outs, freestyles, flexes, dance moments) and pull them from youtube
- an old clip that shows up again in this week's fresh scrape gets a bonus
- prefer real phone or interview footage over film and tv, which gets claimed and muted
</find_the_trend>

<score>
- fresh: plays against that page's usual plays, plays per hour since posting, and whether the same clip or its audio is spreading across pages and platforms
- evergreen: total plays across every copy you found, whether another ai influencer already remade it and beat their usual numbers, and whether it's resurfacing this week
- drop anything older than 7 days in the fresh lane, because pinned posts leak into scrapes
- expect sports broadcasts and press conferences to top the numbers, which is why the gate below decides
</score>

<swap_gate>
- download the top 15 from each lane
- count hard cuts with ffmpeg scene detection, and pass at 0 or 1 in the part you'll use
- make an 8 frame contact sheet and look at it. pass only if one person is on screen most of the time with their face and upper body visible, it's real footage (not a broadcast, a stream overlay or a multi-camera edit), and that person is doing something and is the coolest one in the clip
- if captions, tweet cards or frames are burned in over the person, trace the clean original through the caption credit and use that
- reject anything with a minor as the subject, a private person being humiliated, injury, violence, crime, tragedy, politics, or anything on my no-go list
- show me the top 3 with a frame strip, the scores, who gets replaced, the one-line joke and the cost for each render option, and let me pick
</swap_gate>

<render>
both options take the real clip and the reference sheet with one prompt: "replace [person described by position and clothing] with the man in the image. keep his exact motion, gestures, mouth movement and timing. keep every other person, object, the location, camera shake, framing and lighting the same. no text."

kling 3.0 omni (cheaper, about $0.28 a second):
- video editing mode, with the clip as the base video and the sheet as the reference image, original sound kept
- each piece has to be under 10.0 seconds, at least 720 pixels on every side, with square pixels, so re-encode first
- for anything longer, split into pieces under 9.5 seconds at calm moments where the person is clearly visible, and render every piece with the exact same sheet and prompt
- compare the last frame of each piece with the first frame of the next, and re-render any piece where the face, hair or outfit jumps
- join the pieces with no audio, then lay the original audio back over the whole thing as one track

seedance 2.5 (premium, about $0.97 a second with a video input):
- up to 30 seconds in one pass with no seams and the best consistency
- editing mode with the clip as the reference video and the sheet as the reference image, then lay the original audio back on

never use kling motion control for this, because it rebuilds the whole scene from its image and rejects crowded clips. never use gemini omni edit mode either, because it blocks any video with a real person in it
</render>

<check>
- make a contact sheet of the finished video and look at every frame
- re-render once if the signature feature morphs, anyone except the target changes, text appears that wasn't there, or hands melt at a key moment
- never do more than 2 render attempts without asking me
</check>

<post>
- caption in my language, deadpan, in character, under 6 words, never explaining the joke
- tag the person replaced and the original creator, because that's how the original artist ends up seeing it
- turn on instagram's ai label for the post and the profile, since unlabelled ai accounts lose reach
- fresh clips go out while the original is still inside its week, and evergreen clips go out at the account's best hour
- first comment from the account is "follow for more" or the catchphrase
- never launch or promote a token, and never imply the original person endorsed the character
</post>

<learn>
- log every post with the lane, scores, render option, cost, and plays at 24 and 72 hours
- the next time you run, scrape the account first and fill those columns in
- after 10 posts, compare plays against each score and each lane, shift the weighting toward whatever actually predicted views, and write down what changed
</learn>

<honesty>
- only put numbers on screen or in captions that you scraped or measured
- mark anything you guessed rather than measured
- if no clip passes the gate today, say so instead of forcing a weak one
</honesty>

<deliverables>
- the final mp4 at the source resolution, with the original audio
- the reference sheet
- a short note on why this clip won and why the runners-up lost
- the caption, tags and posting time
- total spend, and anything a human should still check
</deliverables>
```

they can keep working after i close the laptop, argue with each other, reject bad work and finish hundreds of tasks overnight.

but when something can’t be undone, the whole system stops.

6 bots can run the night.

the last stopline is still me.

The killer line: 'a list of places that have not broken yet is a different thing from a list of places that are fine.'
2107157725360615932.text:
OpenAI shipped an agent update that stops reporting what crashed and starts naming the decision that made the crash possible.

A stack trace points at the line that failed. That line is almost never where the problem was introduced.

> WALK - the failure traced backwards through every call that led into it
> BLAME - the commit that introduced each assumption on that path identified
> ECHO - other places in the codebase running on the same assumption flagged
> RANK - the paths sorted by how much live traffic crosses them

Debugging usually ends at the first thing that looks wrong. You patch it, the error disappears, and the cause stays in the repo.

That is why the same bug comes back wearing a different message three weeks later.

The echo step is the uncomfortable one. One bad assumption rarely lives in a single file.

It returns a list of places that have not broken yet, which is a different thing from a list of places that are fine.

A fix without that list is a guess that happened to work. This turns an incident into a map of everything standing on the same floor.

The trace format and the ranking rules are laid out in the breakdown below.

your $20-$200/mo frontier model is researching, writing code, planning…

Jev flips that.

-> which agent goes next?
-> is this worth researching?
-> reply or ignore?
-> publish, wait or escalate?
-> BUY / SELL / HOLD?
-> click this or keep looking?

then I saw the numbers people are reporting and the whole architecture started making a lot more sense.

~1,000 papers classified for around $0.08
~500 emails sorted for around $0.035

browser-agent loops demonstrated around 7 seconds for ~$0.0039

and at the quoted pricing, roughly 10,000 ~1K-token decisions comes out around $0.42.

that’s not because Jev became smarter than Claude.

it’s because nobody asked it to be Claude.

the setup is stupidly simple:

-> big LLM gets the hard thinking, research and writing
-> Jev gets the thousands of tiny decisions between those steps
-> code actually clicks, saves, sends and executes

and suddenly you start noticing these little decisions everywhere.

> your inbox.
> X feed.
> support queue.
> meetings.
> leads.
> video clips.
> browser agents.

that’s the part I think most agent builders are missing.

2107514047578955935.text:
Anthropic opened up a ribosome study and found the machine stalls on purpose, with the pauses doing a job nobody assigned them.

Speed was always the metric. Faster translation, better output, and a stall counted as something gone wrong.

> TIME - translation tracked second by second instead of measured end to end
> MARK - every pause logged with the exact point in the sequence it happened
> SORT - random hesitations separated from pauses that repeat across cells
> FOLD - each repeating pause matched against what the protein was doing then

The pauses are not noise. The same ones land at the same places, in cell after cell, far more often than chance allows.

They cluster where the protein needs a moment. A section finishes folding before the next one is fed out behind it.

Rush that and the chain comes out complete and useless, folded into a shape that does the wrong thing.

So the stall is the instruction. The sequence carries timing information on top of the amino acids everyone reads it for.

Optimising genes for speed has been standard practice for decades. It quietly deletes that timing.

That explains a lot of engineered proteins that are technically correct and biologically dead.

Every repeating pause and what it was waiting for sit in the breakdown below.

2107412258259136869.text:
OpenAI's new system takes one prompt describing a business and returns the places it loses money without anyone noticing.

Nothing about the pitch is examined. It reads the operation as a set of handoffs and looks at what falls through each one.

> MAP - every step from first contact to payment laid out as a chain
> DROP - each handoff measured for what fails to arrive on the other side
> WAIT - the delay between steps counted, because time is its own leak
> OWNER - any step with nobody accountable for it marked immediately
> COST - the losses priced per month instead of described as inefficiency
> ORDER - the leaks ranked by what is cheapest to close first

Consultants start with strategy. Strategy is rarely the problem, and it is always the most expensive thing to change.

The leaks live in the seams. A form that nobody reads, a reply that arrives two days late, a handoff with no owner.

Pricing them is what makes it land. "We lose leads at intake" is an opinion until it has a monthly number attached.

The ordering matters more than the list. Most of these are fixable in an afternoon, and nobody knows which ones.

One prompt in, and what comes back is a repair queue instead of a strategy deck.

The prompt and the leak-pricing method are laid out in the breakdown below.

I GAVE MY BOT $37 IN PAPER MONEY AND ONE RULE: NO ENTRY WITHOUT AN EXIT

$37 → $8,369. 16 simulated hours. The 25x trade made the least money.

Most bots chase the candle. WICK draws three lines before it touches anything: entry, target, stop. If it can't place all three, it doesn't trade.

WICK is a concept agent I designed for perps on BTC, ETH, SOL, AVAX and SUI. In the sim it scans all five, queues the next setup and picks the side on its own.

> Entry, take-profit and stop are on the chart before the order
> Stop sits at -32% ROE, always well before liquidation
> Trades both sides: 6 longs, 1 short
> Closes at target and logs every trade with time, side, leverage and ROE
> Rolls the whole balance into the next trade

That last rule is the entire result, and the reason this stays a simulation. Trade one turned $37 into $89. Trade five turned $883 into $2,006. BTC at 25x made $52 at 02:46. BTC at 20x made $2,367 eleven hours later. Leverage wasn't the edge, compounding was.

Worst moment of the run: a quarter of the way into the SUI long, equity slid 11.3% off the peak. The stop was nowhere near. It held, and SUI closed at +131%.

My favorite moment: the only short of the session. AVAX fell 12%, the position made 96%.

Six closes made $4,336.80. The open ETH long added $3,996.12. $37 + $4,336.80 + $3,996.12 = $8,369.92. Every dollar on the screen has a trade behind it.

25x and 20x are sim settings, not a signal. All-in compounding turns $37 into $8,369 on paper and into zero in real life. Don't copy the sizing.

Hour 16. $8,369 on the screen, an ETH long still open at +91%, and a pixel candle in the corner waiting for the next setup.

2107898724286361928.text:
Anthropic built a model that turns any object into a 3D schematic and then runs experiments on it before anyone touches the real thing.

The geometry was never the hard part. The hard part is a model that knows which parts of the object are allowed to move.

> SHAPE - the object rebuilt as parts with real dimensions, nothing smoothed over
> JOINT - every connection marked with what it permits and what it forbids
> LOAD - forces applied the way the object actually meets them in use
> BREAK - the weakest path traced until something gives, over and over
> SWAP - a single part changed and the whole run repeated from scratch
> RANK - failure modes sorted by how little force it takes to trigger them

A render shows what something looks like. A schematic with constraints shows what it cannot survive.

Simulation tools already do this, and they need weeks of setup by someone who knows the software cold.

Here the setup is the description. The constraints come from what the object is, not from a form someone fills in.

The swap step is where it earns its place. You change one part and get the new failure order in minutes, not days.

Most prototypes exist to find the first thing that breaks. This finds it, then the next four behind it.

Every failure path and the force that caused it sits in the breakdown below.

A Stanford AI professor came up with a way to combine Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol into a unified setup, and this approach completely changes standard concepts of search structure

Most often, cutting-edge neural networks are merged either by dumping prompts into a single shared window or through hardcoded evolutionary cycles. The professor's development completely eliminates human-created rigid search frameworks and separates intellectual labor into distinct layers:

Candidate module: GPT-6.1 Sol explores high-entropy code modifications in secure execution environments

Context isolation: The context window is reset on every iteration to save tokens, while the full tree history is recorded in the graph

Independent evaluation: Candidate code is strictly separated from the validation system, preventing test data leakage and reward function manipulation

Meta-distillation: An offline process analyzes successful patterns and updates guidelines for search directions

> Outperforms current SOTA in Anthropic kernel builder and 11 complex math optimization tasks
> Absolute zero reward hacks: any attempts by the model to cheat metrics or overfit to tests are eliminated

Opus sets the vector of movement along the graph, while Sol verifies hypotheses in code

OpenAI's research system builds the whole thing from one prompt, then writes the report that explains why it is built that way.

Most tools stop at the artifact. You get working output and no record of a single decision inside it.

> FRAME - the prompt turned into the questions the system has to answer
> BUILD - each part made only after the question it answers is written down
> JUSTIFY - every choice logged with the alternative it beat and the reason
> AUDIT - the finished system checked back against the original questions
> WRITE - the report assembled from that log, not from the finished code

Documentation written afterwards is fiction. Nobody remembers why the third option was dropped, so the reasoning gets invented.

Here the record is produced while the decisions are live, which is the only time it is accurate.

The rejected alternatives are the valuable half. Six months later, someone always proposes exactly what was already ruled out.

The audit pass catches the drift. A system that stopped answering its own founding question gets flagged instead of shipped.

One prompt in, and what comes back is not just a build. It is a build you can defend in a room.
```

# CLAUDE. md: Operating manual for my second brain
## Who I am
I am [name]. I work on [your work in one line].
My focus this quarter: [1 to 3 priorities].

You are my chief of staff. I capture. You organize. I decide.
Sort, link, resurface and use my notes. Nothing else.

00_inbox: raw captures. Process them, never leave them here.

60_outputs: drafts, reviews and decisions made from notes.
_system: templates and maps of content. Leave in place.
## Note rules
1. One idea per note. Split captures with several ideas.
2. Filenames lowercase with underscores: pricing_anchors. md
3. Line one: a one sentence summary in bold.
4. Line two: tags. #idea #quote #howto #decision #question #person

6. End every note with a Links section of related [[wikilinks]].
7. When you link A to B, link B back to A.
8. Unsure where it goes? 30_resources, tagged #unsure.
## Safety
1. Never delete. Archive instead.
2. Never edit 50_daily except to add links at the bottom.
3. Moving more than 20 files? Show me the plan first.
4. Cite every note you use as a [[wikilink]].
5. If my notes don't answer it, say so. No filling gaps.
## Weekly review (Sundays)
Read the last 7 days of daily notes and changed notes.
Tell me: what happened, what I keep circling, what I forgot,
which projects stalled, every open loop, and the ONE thing to do next.
If I'm drifting from my focus, say it plainly.
## How I like answers
Answer first. Short. Then the evidence.
No filler. No praise. No "great question".
Quote my notes when it matters.

Anthropic put Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 on the same 3D build task, and the benchmark gap turned out to measure the wrong thing entirely.

Both models produced geometry that passed. Passing is where the similarity ended.

> BRIEF - one identical object description handed to both models, cold
> BUILD - each one produces parts, joints and materials with no further prompting
> OPEN - every output loaded in real software instead of being scored on paper
> BEND - the models pushed until something deforms wrong or a pivot fails
> PRICE - the cost of each run set against how much human cleanup it needed

Haiku 5.5 is the cheaper model by a wide margin, and on a benchmark score the gap looks small.

The gap appears after the file opens. Geometry that scores well can still arrive with pivots in places nothing bends.

Opus 5.5 holds the constraints Haiku drops. Clearances, wall thickness, parts that have to stay separate to move.

That is the number nobody publishes. A cheap run plus two hours of cleanup is not a cheap run.

Benchmarks measure the output. The thing worth measuring is what the output costs you after it exists.
