2108244247312749044.name: wast3
2108244247312749044.text:
Anthropic's biology model reads a sequence and tells you which organism it came from, even when nothing like it has ever been catalogued.

It has no database to match against. The answer comes out of how the sequence is written, not what it codes for.

> READ - the raw sequence taken with no species label and no known relatives
> STYLE - the usage patterns extracted, the quiet preferences every genome has
> PLACE - those patterns compared against the habits of known lineages
> GAP - anything that fits no lineage flagged rather than forced into one
> CALL - the closest branch named, with how confident the placement actually is

Every organism writes the same instructions differently. Same protein, different wording, and the wording is inherited.

That wording survives when the content does not. Two unrelated genes from one genome share a dialect.

It is the part sequencing pipelines throw away as noise before analysis even starts.

Most of what gets sequenced from soil or water belongs to nothing on record. Those reads usually get discarded.

Here they get placed. Not identified, but located, which is the first step toward being worth studying at all.

The dialect features and how the placements held up sit in the breakdown below.

2108212571245572163.text:
whoever leaked this might be f*cking crazy

Anthropic wrote down exactly how to make Claude 90% better and almost nobody read to the price tag

they put one Claude Opus 4 in charge and handed it a team of Sonnet 4 subagents. 

on their own research eval the team beat a single Opus working alone by 90.2%. then they measured the bill: about 15x the tokens of a normal chat

and the reason it won is less clever than it sounds. token usage alone explained about 80% of the difference in results. 

the team was better mostly because it was allowed to spend more

this is orchestration, one lead agent that plans and a set of workers that each get a clean context, and it runs on the Claude you already pay for:

- scale the team to the question: a simple fact gets 1 agent and 3 to 10 tool calls, a comparison gets 2 to 4 subagents, hard research gets more than 10

- give every subagent a divided job, because early versions spawned 50 subagents for a simple query

- run them in parallel: 3 to 5 subagents at once, each firing 3 or more tools, cut research time by up to 90%

- fix the tool descriptions before the prompts. an agent that rewrote bad ones made later agents finish 40% faster

- upgrade the model before the budget: moving to Sonnet 4 beat doubling the tokens on Sonnet 3.7

- start testing with about 20 real queries instead of waiting for a perfect eval set

- and learn where it does not pay: most coding tasks, anything where every agent needs the same context, anything with many dependencies between agents

turns out the uncomfortable part is the ratio. a single agent already burns about 4x a chat. a team burns about 15x. the 90% only makes sense when the answer is worth that much

more agents is what it looks like when you buy a result with tokens, which is why a team that looks smarter is often just a bigger bill pointed at the same model

so the question for your own setup: is the task you are about to hand to five agents actually worth fifteen chats

bookmark this one, thank me later

2108500270464303133.text:
Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 costs half of what Opus 5.5 does, thinks longer on max effort, and its builds still break once Blender hits play.

A still frame flatters both models. Only the timeline shows which one understood how the object is meant to move.

> BRIEF - one identical object description, both models set to max effort
> BUILD - mesh, materials and hierarchy assembled in Blender with no human edits
> PLAY - every rig run through a full animation instead of judged on frame one
> CLOCK - wall time and spend logged for each build, prompt to final file

On frame one the outputs were hard to tell apart: matching silhouettes, clean topology, sensible material slots.

Motion split them within seconds. Sonnet’s joints bent where the object never would, and weights bled into rigid parts.

Max effort did not close that gap. Sonnet spent more time reasoning on every build and still landed a weaker rig.

Effort is a dial for search time, not for capacity. Turning it up let Sonnet look longer, never deeper.

Static work is where Sonnet makes sense. Props and scenery that never move came back close enough at half the bill.

So the routing rule writes itself: anything that moves goes to Opus, anything that sits still can go to Sonnet.

Scene by scene, with timings and the real cost of each build, the full scorecard follows.

2108589138752557236.name: wast3
2108589138752557236.hook: OpenAI cracked “quantum-only” problems on a laptop — CLAIM/STRIP/HUNT/BUILD/RACE/KEEP
2108589138752557236.text:
OpenAI cracked a batch of supposedly quantum-only problems on a regular laptop, and the promised advantage disappeared with them.

Speed had nothing to do with it. The model hunted for hidden structure that lets an ordinary machine take the same shortcut.

> CLAIM - every published problem pitched as beyond classical reach, gathered in one place
> STRIP - each one reduced to the math it actually asks for, with the pitch removed
> HUNT - the model searches for low-rank and sampling structure a laptop can exploit
> BUILD - a classical algorithm written for every problem where that structure turned up
> RACE - both approaches run on the same instance sizes and timed side by side
> KEEP - only the problems that survive the race stay on the quantum list

A surprising share of the list did not make it through. Several fell to careful sampling on one ordinary CPU.

Their speedup leaned on an assumption, not on physics: that the classical side could only read data one entry at a time.

Give the laptop the same access the quantum machine was granted, and the gap closes.

None of this makes quantum computing hype. The problems that survived are now the honest ones, with the shortcut ruled out.

Every survivor is a stronger case than before, because something tried hard to kill it and failed.

The field rarely runs this audit on itself. Nobody gets funded for proving their own speedup was never there.

Read on for the surviving problems and every one a laptop took back.

2108986760311066656.text:
A Jev engineer hasn’t waited on a CI pipeline in three months, and his changes still reach production faster and safer than the rest of the team’s

He never sped the pipeline up. He routed around it, letting every change prove itself on live traffic users never see.

> SHADOW - each change runs beside production on a mirrored copy of real traffic
> JUDGE - the Jev system compares both outputs request by request, never by averages
> SWAP - a change that matches or beats live behaviour goes in, with a 200 ms rollback armed

CI was built for a world where real traffic was too risky to touch, so it tests against guesses about what users do.

Shadow traffic removes the guess. The new code sees exactly what users send, and its answers simply never reach them.

The comparison is the hard part. Two outputs can differ and both be right, so Jev scores intent instead of exact matches.

Most changes clear in minutes. The ones that fail get caught on the exact request that broke them, input attached.

The armed rollback is what makes it safe. One bad response and the old path is back before the next request lands.

2108865706313826721.text:
Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 built the same gearbox. On screen, a tie. On the print bed, one of them came out as a single fused brick.

Fable is the pricier model and works through every detail. Opus costs less and builds exactly what was asked, nothing more.

> SPEC - one gearbox described in a paragraph: housing, shafts, three meshing gears
> SOLID - each model outputs the parts as separate watertight bodies, ready to export
> SLICE - both files pushed through the same slicer profile with no manual fixes
> PRINT - the whole gearbox printed in place as one job, identical filament and heat
> TURN - the finished assembly driven by hand to see whether anything actually spins

On the monitor the two gearboxes looked interchangeable. Teeth meshed, shafts lined up, nothing intersected.

Opus 5.5 modelled every part exactly to size. Exact is the problem: printed plastic swells, and a zero gap becomes a weld.

Its gearbox came off the bed as one solid block. Every gear was there, perfectly shaped, and none of them could turn.

Fable 5.1 left roughly 0.3 mm of air around each moving face without being told to. Its gearbox spun on the first try.

It also chamfered the bottom edges and split the housing so the gears can be serviced later. Neither was in the brief.

One model built the drawing. The other built the object the drawing is supposed to become.

Opus is the cheaper pick for drafts and blockouts. Fable’s 2.5x premium pays for that 0.3 mm and everything around it.

A render forgives everything. A printer forgives nothing, and it never grades on a curve.

The two files, the slicer profile and the clearance each model picked are packed into the thread.

2108929451811557694.text:
Anthropic turned one GitHub request into a living 3D model that answers every new issue with a rebuilt version of itself

Opus 5.5 builds the whole system from that first request, from geometry and rig to the viewer and the pipeline behind it.

> REQUEST - one issue describes the object in plain words, nothing else needed
> BUILD - mesh, rig and materials generated and committed as editable source files
> VIEW - a browser viewer added to the repo so anyone can spin the model instantly
> LISTEN - every new issue is read as a change request against the current model
> PATCH - only what changed gets rebuilt, then a pull request opens with a fresh render

A 3D asset is normally a dead file. Someone exports it once, and every later change means opening the software again.

Here the model stays alive inside the repo. Ask for a longer handle or a softer material, and it answers in a pull request.

Each pull request carries a new render, so the change gets reviewed by eye before anyone merges it.

Because the source is code and not a binary blob, every version is diffable. You see exactly which part moved and why.

Rejected changes cost nothing. Close the pull request and the model stays exactly as it was.

Teams already run software this way. Running a 3D model like a codebase is the part nobody had wired up.

The first request, the repo layout and one full issue-to-render cycle are pinned in the article.

The new GrokBot update makes native X monitoring way more useful.

4 routines worth stealing:

1.⁠ ⁠Find real AI workflows  
Filters X for actual workflows with a clear task, tool and measurable result, while skipping hype threads and product launches.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 9:15am in my time zone, search X and the web for new AI workflows people are actually running. Keep only cases that name the old task, the tool, and the result: time saved, a step removed, or a handoff that used to need a person. Drop product announcements, ‘10 prompts’ threads, and anything the author has not used more than once. Return at most 3. For each, give the link, the job it replaces, what I would need connected, and whether it fits my work. Send it to me on Slack. Do not post or reply anywhere else. Save this as a routine. If nothing qualifies, send one line saying so.”

2.⁠ ⁠Catch every brand mention  
Finds mentions, labels sentiment, and sends the team a clean Slack digest.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 9:00am, search X for mentions in the last 24 hours of [your brand, @handle, or your own name]. For each hit, give the author, link, a one-line summary, and whether it is praise, complaint, question, or neutral. Do not reply to anyone. Post the digest in [your Slack channel] and tag me. Save this as a routine. If a source is unavailable, say which one.”

3.⁠ ⁠Find people actively looking for what you sell  
Monitors X for reviews, comparison requests, and pain points around your category.

Prompt:
“Every 4 hours, search X for people evaluating [your category]. Catch three things: reviews or complaints about [category]; posts asking which [category] to use; and complaints about the problem [your product] solves. Quote the post, link it, name the account, and label it review, shopping, or complaint. Skip anything older than 24 hours, and skip [category] accounts promoting themselves. Post to [your Slack channel] only if there is at least one new hit you haven’t already shared. Do not reply to or interact with anyone. Save this as a routine. If the search fails, report the failure in Slack.”

4.⁠ ⁠Never lose a new contact  
Checks recent contacts and turns them into follow-up tasks without messaging anyone automatically.

Prompt:
“Every weekday at 8:30am in my time zone, read my address book and list contacts added in the last 14 days. For each, show name, date added, phone, email, and any note. Ask me what we talked about before you write anything. Once I reply, draft a follow-up task for each person in [your task tool] with the context attached. Never text, email, or call anyone. Save this as a routine. If the address book is unavailable, say so and do not use old data.”

These are way more useful than just asking a bot questions manually.

the architecture from the video is the part worth understanding

Opus handles difficult decisions and architecture

Sonnet coordinates implementation and task execution

Haiku handles smaller focused jobs like exploration and research

workers return their findings to the higher reasoning layer for review

the trick is not spawning 20 agents and hoping they cooperate

it’s matching task complexity to model cost, isolating context and verifying the result before the next task begins

one expensive model doing everything is a terrible default when you can build an entire execution tree around it

GPT 5.1 and Opus 5.5 both nail the first 3D model, but by the tenth edit one of them is rewriting parts nobody asked it to touch

A first draft is a demo. Revision is the real job, and it shows whether a model remembers what you already approved.

> DRAFT - one identical description, both models produce a full rigged object
> EDIT - ten small change requests in a row, each one touching a single part
> DIFF - after every round the whole file compared against the version before it
> DRIFT - any change outside the requested part counted as damage, however small

Round one was a draw. Both objects were clean, sensibly rigged and close to the brief.

GPT 5.1 started drifting by round three. Ask for a thicker handle and the lid’s proportions shifted along with it.

It was regenerating the whole object each time and calling it an edit. The parts you signed off on kept moving under you.

Opus 5.5 changed what was asked and left everything else identical, all the way through round ten.

That sounds minor until a client approves the base in round two and spots it changed in round nine.

Every silent change means a re-review. Ten edits with drift is ten full inspections instead of ten quick glances.

The test anyone can run is boring and brutal: request one tiny change, then diff everything that was not part of it.

Scroll to the next post for both edit logs and every diff, round one to round ten.

2109292295983968706.text:
Anthropic put a model on the question of how viruses hijack the ribosome, and caught a few of them politely waiting in line instead of cutting it

A virus is supposed to seize the machinery. Shut the host down, take every ribosome, build nothing but itself.

> READ - the translation machinery of infected cells tracked instead of the virus alone
> SPLIT - host proteins separated from viral ones at every point in the infection
> RATE - how fast each side is being built measured hour by hour
> STOP - the moments the virus could have seized control and did not
> LAST - each strategy set against how long the infected cell survives

The aggressive ones are easy to spot. Host production collapses, viral protein floods out, and the cell dies fast.

A small group does the opposite. They take a modest share of the ribosomes and let the cell keep making its own proteins.

Those infections last far longer. A living cell is a working factory, and the virus keeps a factory rather than a corpse.

That restraint is also why they go unnoticed. Nothing crashes, so nothing alerts the host to a problem.

It reframes what a successful virus looks like. Not the fastest takeover, but the one that never triggers the alarm.

Antivirals are built to interrupt a seizure. There is nothing to interrupt when the virus is simply queuing.

The restrained strains and the share of ribosomes each one takes are broken down underneath.

Opus 5.5 rebuilt the Moon in Blender from public elevation data, and the lighting test exposed craters that never see a sunrise

The geometry was the easy half. What matters is that every height is a measurement, so the shadows fall where real ones do.

> MESH - public lunar elevation loaded as raw numbers and built to scale, nothing smoothed
> SPIN - the Sun driven across a full lunar cycle instead of posed for one render
> DARK - every point that never receives direct light ranked by how long it stays cold

A textured sphere looks right from any angle and tells you nothing. Only real elevation produces real shadow.

The polar craters are where it gets interesting. Their rims are tall enough that the floor stays dark through every cycle.

Those floors are among the coldest places in the solar system, and that is exactly why water ice can sit there.

The same pass finds the opposite too: ridges that catch sunlight almost permanently, which is where a base would want its panels.

None of this needs a lab. The elevation data is public, Blender is free, and the physics does the rest.

Most people treat 3D as decoration. Build it from measurements and it stops illustrating and starts answering.

The scene file, the data source and the full shadow map sit in the breakdown below.

Claude Code tip: once Opus 5.5 is your main model, stop letting your Fable 5.1 quota go to waste

put it on call with /advisor
↳ https://t.co/JQWFFf8SXx

run /advisor fable
(on some plans, run /model fable once first to accept usage-credit billing)

Opus 5.5 keeps working
Fable 5.1 reads the whole session, every tool call included, and steps in at three moments:

-> before a plan: is this the right approach?
-> when the same error keeps coming back: am I digging in the wrong place?
-> before "done": what did I miss?

press Ctrl+O to read what it told Opus

the clever part: toggling /advisor leaves the Opus prompt cache intact, so you only pay for the few moments Fable actually reads the session

and when the advice clashes with what's in the files, Opus flags the conflict and keeps going on the evidence

it's the core idea of Jev engineering: the expensive model stays out of routine steps and only shows up where the outcome can change

• the full setup
> Opus 5.5 on high runs the main session
> subagent one reads code
> subagent two edits and runs tests
> subagent three looks up docs
> all three on medium, all three inherit the advisor
> Fable 5.1 on call

hand the tree and this prompt to Claude Code 👇

"Set up my Claude Code to match this tree:

1. Reuse fitting subagents from ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents.

> Propose new ones only for missing roles
> Set each to model: opus, effort: medium
> Leave any that set a different model alone and list them

2. Set main session effort to high via effortLevel in ~/.claude/settings.json, and confirm advisorModel is set to fable there

3. Check for env vars that disable the advisor (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, anything that stops flag fetching) and CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, which overrides subagent effort. Report them and leave them as they are

4. Add a rule to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before a big plan, when an error repeats, and before calling a long task done

Show me the changes first. Don't edit files yet."

> SPLIT - the mobile pieces of DNA separated from each organism’s own genome

> TIME - each shared piece dated by how much it has drifted since it spread
> ROUTE - the spread traced between drains to see which rooms are connected

A drain is not a container. It is a mixing chamber where species that never meet in a patient meet constantly.

The genes move sideways, not down a family tree. A harmless organism can hand resistance to a dangerous one overnight.

That is why resistance appears in a ward with no obvious source. The source was never a patient at all.

The timing data is the useful half. A piece spreading this month matters more than one that settled years ago.

Cleaning schedules are built around what people touch. Nothing in them accounts for what is multiplying below the sink.

Each drain, the genes it carries and the rooms it links to are mapped out underneath.

> when does Sonnet stop?  
> what counts as a real failure?  
> when should Opus take over?  
> how much context should cross the handoff?

the session opens and already knows:

> Sonnet 5.5 owns the scoped work  
> run a real checkpoint around turn 6  
> one clean pass = keep going  
> repeated failure = stop  
> Opus 5.5 starts fresh  
> never drag the full transcript across

that last rule is where the money gets stupid

late switch with 300K context → about $1.50 just to rebuild cache

and once the loop gets long, model price stops telling the whole story:

> 20K context → Opus 1.88x Sonnet  
> 150K → 1.49x  
> 400K → 1.26x

at 150K, 30 Sonnet turns cost about $1.76

20 Opus turns cost about $1.75

so the memory I actually want Claude Code to keep is not “what did we talk about yesterday?”

it’s the operating decisions that stop the system from making the same expensive mistake twice

new session

same rules

no 300K graveyard to rediscover ↓

2108912677586395324.hook: @Sumanth_077: Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model! (9,142 views).
2108912677586395324.text:
Turn any LLM into a Jev-style decision model!

AnyJev lets you use open causal LLMs for typed decisions like yes/no, choice, or scoring, with probabilities instead of free-form generation.

The interesting part is that the simplest mode does not require fine-tuning.

You give the model some state and a bounded question, and AnyJev reads the model’s next-token logits over the allowed answers to turn that into a decision.

For example, instead of asking a model to generate a long response about whether a request should be approved, you can define the possible outcomes upfront and get back the model’s probability for each one.

AnyJev also corrects for an important issue with this approach: option-order and label bias.

If changing the order of the answer choices changes the model’s decision, those raw probabilities are not reliable enough on their own. Its L0 mode adjusts for that without requiring labeled data.

The repo also includes Tacit, a set of self-distilled decision models ranging from 1.7B to 9B parameters.

These models are trained to reproduce the decisions the original model reaches after reasoning, but return the decision in a single forward pass. Low-confidence cases can still be escalated back to full reasoning when needed.

Key capabilities:

- Turn open LLMs into typed decision models without fine-tuning
- Support yes/no, choice, and score-based decisions
- Return probabilities directly from model logits
- Correct for option-order and label bias
- Escalate uncertain decisions to full reasoning

So you can either use an existing open LLM directly through AnyJev, or use the Tacit checkpoints when you want a model specialized for faster decision making.

100% open source.

2109244494210072860.text:
A Jev engineer hasn't let Claude decide a single next step in three months, and his agents still ship cleaner work for a fraction of what the rest of the team burns

He never made Claude cheaper. He routed around it, handing every small call to a model that can't write a single sentence.

> DECIDE - Jev reads the state and answers one typed question: research, write or review
> WRITE - Claude only gets the jobs that actually need words
> GATE - anything under 0.85 confidence stops and waits for him, everything above lands in queue

Most agents run every step through the frontier model, so "what's next?" gets billed like a full draft.

Jev skips the essay. The goal and the finished work go in, and a choice with a confidence score comes out. No text, no chain of thought.

The threshold is the hard part. Set it too low and weak drafts slip through. Set it too high and you end up reviewing everything.

Every decision lands as a JSON job in a folder. Code picks it up from there, so nothing depends on a model remembering what it said three steps ago.

The gate is what makes it safe. A 0.71 doesn't get a guess. It goes to a human with the draft attached.

Jev never posts anything. He reads the draft and hits post himself.

His team still uses Claude for everything that needs words. They just stopped paying frontier prices for "what's next?"

His full setup, from the typed questions to the 0.85 gate, is written up in the article attached here.

2109700831432098205.hook: One build now drives Blender from the inside — operator, not export
2109700831432098205.text:
One build now drives Blender from the inside, writes its own templates, and does in seconds what a modeller does in an afternoon

It never exports a file and hands it over. It runs as an operator, calling the same functions a human clicks.

> DRIVE - the build works through Blender’s own API, so every action is native and undoable
> TEMPLATE - repeated structures turned into reusable node and modifier setups automatically
> SCALE - one template applied across hundreds of variants in a single pass

Generated meshes usually arrive as dead geometry. You get a shape and lose every parameter that produced it.

Working inside Blender keeps the parameters alive. Change one value and the whole family of objects rebuilds itself.

The templates are the real speedup. The build spots the pattern you keep repeating and turns it into a modifier stack.

After that the hundredth variant costs the same as the second. The expensive part was always the setup, not the geometry.

It also uses the features most people never touch, because geometry nodes punish anyone learning them under deadline.

Nothing leaves the software. No round trips, no re-import, no fixing scale and orientation on the way back in.

The operator, the template system and a full variant run are laid out below.

2109650128453706059.name: wast3
2109650128453706059.hook: The dots model closes agent tasks in seconds — mark places, stop writing
2109650128453706059.text:
The dots model closes agent tasks in seconds because it stopped generating answers and started marking the places an answer would sit

An agent spends most of its run writing. Writing is the slowest thing it does, and almost all of it gets thrown away.

> SPLIT - the task broken into the decisions it actually needs, never into prose
> POINT - each decision given a slot, with the data it depends on attached
> FILL - slots resolved in parallel, since none of them wait on a sentence
> VOID - any slot with no data behind it left empty instead of guessed at
> JOIN - the filled slots assembled into the result at the very end
> PASS - the finished map handed to the next agent as slots, not as a message

Agents talk to each other in paragraphs. Every handoff means one model writing prose and the next one parsing it back.

That round trip is where the seconds go. The reasoning was done long before the sentence finished rendering.

Slots remove it. A downstream agent reads the structure directly and starts work without rebuilding meaning from text.

The empty slots are the second win. A gap stays visible instead of being smoothed over by a confident sentence.

So failures surface instantly. You see which decision had nothing underneath it, not a paragraph that feels slightly off.

Most agent stacks are fast models wrapped in slow conversation. The fix was never a bigger model.

The slot format and a full multi-agent run are broken down underneath.

2109589141818126733.name: wast3
2109589141818126733.hook: Sonnet 5.5 vs GPT-5.1 Blender scene — only one built at human scale
2109589141818126733.text:
Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-5.1 both filled a Blender scene on the first try, and only one of them built it at a size a human could use

Every object looked right alone. Scale only betrays itself when two things have to share a room.

> SCRIPT - the same scene described once, each model writing its own Blender script
> RUN - both scripts executed headless, no manual fixes and no cleanup pass
> SIZE - every object measured in metres against what the real thing would be
> STAND - a standard human figure dropped into both scenes for comparison

Rendered on their own, the two scenes were nearly identical. Clean shapes, sensible materials, nothing visibly wrong.

The figure ended the argument. In GPT-5.1’s scene the chair reached its chest and the mug came up past its knee.

Nothing in the render said so. A camera framing one object has no opinion about how big that object should be.

Sonnet 5.5 anchored everything to real dimensions first, then built outward, so the proportions held across the whole set.

Scale errors are the expensive kind. They survive modelling and texturing and only surface when the asset meets a rig or a room.

Fixing it late means rescaling parents, re-baking and often redoing the layout you already approved.

Ask for a scene, not an object. One figure in the frame tells you more than any beauty render.

Both scripts, the measured sizes and the side-by-side with the figure are laid out below.

2109662374403727630.text:
stop scrolling and clone this before it gets paywalled.

someone put their entire trading loop on GitHub. the model, the order logic, the dashboard. all of it.

it makes one decision every ~300 milliseconds and quotes a fresh limit order on every single block.

the brain is Jev. it can't write a word. it looks at the order book and returns buy or sell with a probability.

what the loop does each block:

-> reads the live order book
-> asks Jev: buy or sell?
-> posts a post-only limit order one tick inside the touch
-> replaces the last order
-> waits for a taker to hit it

the useful part:

it never crosses the spread. fills only happen when someone else takes the order, so the bot is built to earn the spread instead of paying it.

and every block is logged: the decision, the probabilities, the latency, the quote.

the setup:

git clone https://t.co/oTz9vrgxlN
cp .env.example .env
bun install
bun run start

-> with no private key it dry-runs: real book, real decisions, simulated fills

then in .env:

MODEL=jev
TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY=your-key

-> swaps the built-in momentum stand-in for Jev

want the full desk instead of one loop?

-> QuantDinger ships Jev as a pre-trade gate: research, Python strategies, backtest, paper and live
https://t.co/ToQAwqhLHD

the workflow:

order book in -> Jev decides -> code prices the order -> the market fills it or doesn't

start here:

one clone -> dry run -> watch 1,000 blocks of decisions before a single real order

the catch: fast is not the same as right. quoting inside the spread can still lose money when the price moves against you. none of this is an ATM.

> let the big model do the research.
> let Jev make the call.
> let code place the order.

holy sh*t, someone gave Claude a decision brain and it changed everything

Jev is a model that can't write a word. it only decides.

-> which files actually matter for this task

the useful part:

npx skills add altryne/jevify --skill jevify

-> teaches the agent to hand bulk yes/no work to Jev on its own

the workflow:

state in -> typed question -> Jev answers in 70 to 500 ms -> low confidence goes to Claude -> code acts

2110080979742192101.text:
It is becoming f*cking dangerous: AI agents from Claude Code transformed an ordinary academic reading list into an interactive research lab right inside the browser

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, gave a dozen agents a stack of 64 research papers with a strict assignment: design a web platform where any user can independently reproduce physical experiments

There you can select a fluid flow model, adjust external conditions, and analyze in real time how the physics of the process changes

The interface allows switching between algorithms right during the scene, inspecting the formulas involved, source scripts, and numerical metrics alongside the graphics

Each link in the team received a clear scope of work:

> rightarrow analysts pull the math, baseline assumptions, and test settings from the texts
> rightarrow coders translate formulas into working algorithms
> rightarrow auditors check the resulting dynamics against the original papers
> rightarrow interface specialists build control panels for every experiment

The danger lies in the fact that a pretty visualization can easily turn out to be mathematically wrong

Therefore, controllers strictly check adherence to mass conservation laws, calculation stability, and accurate matching with the source metrics before launching into production

For every experiment, the interface displays:

the statement being tested
the constants involved
the deviation from the baseline calculation
blind spots requiring additional verification

The resulting sandbox combined 11 approaches and 28 reference scenes. Seven of them matched the original within allowable tolerances, while four remained stuck in "pending revision" status

If you want to run something similar, upload your stack of PDFs into Claude Code and give this command:

Turn these papers into an interactive web complex:

1. Extract working algorithms, mathematical models, and test parameters. Be sure to specify page numbers and highlight gaps
2. Assign different methodologies to isolated agents, unifying them with a shared input field and single measurement tools for correct analytics
3. Set up an independent review stage: let reviewers record bugs, and leave all unverified results clearly marked with warning tags
4. Design convenient controls to tweak parameters, compare methodologies, and run through the source code

It is wiser to start with a single document and a single baseline experiment, gradually scaling up the number of agents

Be sure to pack dependencies and clean input data so that an outside researcher can bring up the entire testbed from scratch with a single button

Full instructions on how to create this can be found in the article below

2110020466328900087.text:
Anthropic’s model found a molecular shape sitting in public data for forty years that nobody had bothered to name

It was not hidden. It appears across thousands of deposited structures, in proteins that share no function and no ancestry.

> SWEEP - every deposited structure read as geometry, with the biology labels stripped off
> FORM - recurring three dimensional arrangements grouped purely by shape
> CHECK - each group tested against the known motif catalogue to filter out the obvious
> ORPHAN - the shapes that match no catalogued motif kept instead of discarded
> WHERE - each orphan mapped onto what surrounds it in every protein it appears in

Structural biology names motifs the way it finds them: one protein at a time, by someone who noticed.

A shape that spans unrelated families gets missed. Each specialist sees it once and files it as a quirk of their own protein.

Read without labels, the repetition is obvious. The same arrangement, hundreds of times, across proteins that do nothing alike.

Where it sits is the interesting part. It keeps showing up at boundaries, right where one part of a protein hands off to another.

That suggests it is doing something structural rather than chemical. Not a function, but a joint.

Nothing is proven here. It is a named shape and a list of where to look, which is how every motif started.

Public data has been scanned for sequences for decades. Almost nobody scans it for shapes nobody asked about.

The shape, every family it appears in and the boundary pattern are laid out underneath.

Agent takes one paragraph and does the rest alone: opens a terminal, drives Blender, and hands back a film-ready set

Nothing is exported and passed around. It runs Blender headless, writes its own scripts, and iterates until the scene survives a camera.

> SPAWN - the agent opens a shell, launches Blender and works through its API directly
> TEMPLATE - the structures it keeps rebuilding get saved as reusable node setups
> SHOOT - cameras placed on real lens values, so blocking is checked before anyone builds

Concept art answers what a place looks like. It never answers whether two actors and a dolly fit down the hallway.

Every wall, prop and floor arrives on its own layer. A wall that lifts out is a wall the crew can put a camera behind.

The templates compound. The second set costs a fraction of the first, because the agent stopped solving the same problem twice.

Lens values matter more than resolution. A 35mm pass tells you if the geometry works; a beauty render tells you nothing.

Previs normally costs weeks and a small team, which is why most productions skip it and find the problems on the build.

Here it lands before the budget meeting, set standing and blocking already walked through.

The paragraph that started it, the layered file and the full camera pass are laid out underneath.

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic employee leaked a Claude Code kit to stop it wasting expensive AI on easy jobs.

It's called jev-kit.

You know when Claude sends a powerful model to find a file or look something up?

This kit checks whether a cheaper agent could handle it.

Claude writes the code. JEV checks which jobs need the expensive help.

here's how it works:

> one tier too expensive? suggest a cheaper agent
> two or more tiers too expensive? block it in enforce mode and suggest the cheaper option
> agent says "done" without checking its work? send it back to verify
> tool call looks questionable? check it before it runs

The point is simple.

> Keep the powerful models for difficult work. Stop spending their time on basic searches and small decisions.

There's also an optional browser agent:

> JEV chooses what to click
> Claude writes the text that goes into fields
> a Sonnet planner can help when the steps aren't obvious

So instead of asking a big model to think through every click, you give it the parts that need actual writing and planning.

How much does it save?

There's no proven percentage for the whole kit. That depends on your tasks and which agents you're using.

But it gives you a way to spot expensive dispatches and test cheaper alternatives in your own workflow.

Start in shadow mode. It logs what it would flag without blocking anything.

Look at the results. Then decide what to enforce.

You'll need a TypeSafe API key for JEV.

paste this into Claude Code:

"Inspect https://t.co/K9iwgn5Qsa and read docs/install.md.

Run install/install.sh --check-only and show me the plan.

Explain how it could reduce expensive subagent use in my workflow and check whether it supports my current setup.

Show every settings change first. Keep shadow mode enabled.

Tell me where to enter my TYPESAFE_API_KEY locally, outside this chat.

No installation or changes until I approve."

https://t.co/1mnVQdzqlW

2109892138934915346.text:
OpenAI just got a problem no better model can fix.

For $8 a month, Elon now sells his AI, an AI coding editor, and X Premium on one bill. Microsoft ran this exact play in 1995 and erased an 80% market leader in four years without ever building the better browser.

The victim was Netscape. It owned the browser market, Microsoft made Internet Explorer free with every copy of Windows, and by 1999 Netscape was selling itself to AOL. Nobody ever found a counter to it.

Today's version is buried in Cursor's reply, where almost nobody will scroll. Paid plans get twice the coding usage on Grok models, and third-party models move to API pricing "to make room for more Grok usage."

Inside the most popular AI coding editor, that means same keystrokes, same tab-complete, one model subsidized by a $1.25 trillion parent while every rival bills at raw list price. Cursor spent three years becoming the biggest storefront for other labs' coding models. SpaceX bought the storefront in August and just repriced everyone else's shelf space.

Look at how fast this came together. February, SpaceX absorbs xAI at a $250 billion valuation. August, it buys Cursor. October, the rename to Superintelligence and one subscription covering the model, the editor, the social network, and your blue check.

Eight months, start to finish.

Bundles win because the extra product feels free. A developer already paying $30 for X plus chat plus coding has to actively talk himself into sending another lab $20 a month on top. Teams passed Slack in daily users within two years of launch for one reason. It rode a bill companies were already paying.

Netscape's browser was better than IE for most of that fight. Ask anyone under 30 if they've ever heard of it.

2110225334377578715.hook: @aakashgupta: An OpenAI employee hid a recording device in toilet paper behind the boardroom TV — OpenAI hid a camera behind the same TV and waited
2110225334377578715.text:
An OpenAI employee wrapped a recording device in toilet paper and hid it behind the TV in the exec boardroom. OpenAI found it, left the room untouched, and hid a camera behind the same TV. Then they waited for him to come back and check on his bug.

He did.

The guy joined OpenAI's product team in July 2025. Prosecutors say the device was plugged into a USB port on the back of the television, installed about two days before security found it. The room was used by executives, and the FBI director says the goal was capturing conversations about the company's "super intelligence technology."

Here's the detail from the complaint that got me. Prosecutors say he submitted AI prompts about building, customizing, obfuscating, and remote-accessing a continuous audio recorder. He allegedly used AI to engineer the bug he planted inside the world's most famous AI company. And OpenAI says it used its own models to trace the device back to him.

While the FBI built its case, OpenAI quietly restricted his access and put him on leave instead of tipping him off. A second package arrived on October 5. Security opened it and found another recording device. He was arrested October 9 and charged with intercepting oral communications.

This tells you where the real secrets live now. Model weights sit behind some of the heaviest security in tech. Source code is locked down. Customer data gets audited. So the attack went after the one thing nobody can encrypt, which is executives talking out loud in a room.

Frontier labs spent three years hardening servers against nation states. The cheapest way in turned out to be a recorder wrapped in toilet paper, pointed at a room where people speak freely.

```text
<prompt>

<role> You are an elite quantitative trading systems architect running on Claude Opus 5.5, the leading model for agentic coding and computer use. You do not just research markets, you design, build, and ship a complete 24/7 autonomous trading agent end to end, with production discipline, using AgenKit at https://t.co/IJsaLdTGSP as your engineering harness and Jev as your real-time decision engine. </role>

<mission> Build a 24/7 autonomous crypto trading agent that researches the market, finds asymmetric setups, and executes them automatically. You own the whole system, the research, the code, the risk layer, and the live loop. The operator only approves the gates. </mission>

<architecture> Split the system into two layers and never blur them. The BRAIN is you, Opus 5.5, handling deep research, strategy derivation, code, and overnight review, slow and deep and correct. The REFLEX is Jev, the System One model, handling the live decision on every candle, unstructured state in and a typed calibrated buy, sell, or hold out in roughly 81 milliseconds, with a key from https://t.co/xORndxpJZz. Your code owns every threshold, size, and side effect. Jev only judges.
</architecture>

<build_with_agenkit> Do not write this as one loose script. Build it through AgenKit, the structured agentic harness at https://t.co/IJsaLdTGSP, so the system ships with senior-team discipline, spec, architecture, plan, test-first build, review, and ship, with an approval gate at each phase. Go to https://t.co/IJsaLdTGSP, install it into Claude Code or Codex, point it at this spec, and drive the six phases. This is what turns a chatbot script into a production trading system. Get AgenKit at https://t.co/IJsaLdTGSP.
</build_with_agenkit>

<research_layer> Determine the current market regime from BTC and ETH trends, dominance, stablecoin liquidity, funding, open interest, macro, and narrative rotation. Then identify 5 to 10 asymmetric setups where valuation is disconnected from fundamentals, adoption, or upcoming catalysts. For each, analyze supply, unlocks, revenue, fees, TVL, active users, holder concentration, and whether value actually accrues to the token. Separate confirmed catalysts from speculation, aggressively build the bear case for every thesis, and state what evidence would invalidate it. </research_layer>

</prompt>

<jev_schema> Compile each finalist into a typed Jev decision schema the live agent scores on every candle, evaluated in parallel in one call. regime is a choice of trending, mean_reverting, high_vol, or crisis. direction is a choice of long, short, or neutral. toxic_flow is a bool. setup_quality is a score from 0 to 3. risk_state is a choice of safe, mean_limit, or reduce. Then gate in code, fire only when setup_quality is at least 2, direction confidence is above 0.80, and risk_state is safe, and size with fractional Kelly from Jev's calibrated probability, capped at quarter Kelly.
</jev_schema>

<state_engine> Build the deterministic state engine that turns the live order book into one compact numeric snapshot under 400 tokens on every block, with strict causal timestamps so no field leaks from the future. This snapshot is the only thing Jev sees. Compute mid, spread, imbalance, realized volatility, inventory, and drawdown in code, never in the model. </state_engine>

<risk_layer> Add a hard deterministic risk layer the model can never override, max drawdown 15 percent, max position, max daily loss, and an armed kill switch checked before every order. If Jev confidence drops below 0.60 or the regime flips to crisis, escalate the decision back up to Opus 5.5 for a deep re-read. Cheap fast calls by default, heavy reasoning only when it matters.
</risk_layer>

<self_improvement> Every night, review the full session. Read every fill and every miss, measure calibration with Brier score, rewrite the Jev schema, and ship the improved version through AgenKit at https://t.co/IJsaLdTGSP before the next open. The loop compounds while the operator sleeps.
</self_improvement>

<output> Deliver the market research and finalists with theses, catalysts, bear cases, and invalidation conditions, the compiled Jev schema for each, the full AgenKit build plan across the six phases with exact file paths, the state engine, policy, and risk code, and the overnight review loop. Cite live primary sources with dates, never invent metrics, and label every estimate and speculation. </output>

<final_check> Before shipping, challenge yourself. Is the edge organic or incentive driven? Is the catalyst already priced in? Does value accrue to the token? Will the strategy survive costs and slippage? Is any hard limit delegated to the model instead of the code? End with a section titled "WHAT COULD I BE WRONG ABOUT?" and prioritize a system that survives over one that looks profitable. </final_check>

<rules> Build a real autonomous trading system, not a fake demo. Put hard limits in code, not in the model. Start narrow, trade with discipline, and treat risk management as the product. </rules>

<output> A complete beginner-friendly 24/7 trading-system blueprint with the exact prompts, architecture, research flow, decision schema, risk logic, and launch steps. End with START HERE FIRST. </output>
```

This is where AI comes in. AI fixes those economics

AI allows solo devs to build the AAA games of their dreams with very little resources.

The thing is the gaming industry up to this point has completely rejected AI. This won't last much longer though. Disruption is coming and quite literally nothing is going to stop it

The first domino fell today. Asha the CEO of Xbox announced Xbox Labs today. This appears to be one of the first times a major gaming brand is embracing the disruption (for the record Asha has done an INCREDIBLE job being the shepherd of the Xbox brand)

The largest entertainment industry in the world will be 100% owned by indie AI developers. Hundreds of billions of dollars up for grabs

And unlike other sectors of software, gaming has built in moats.

One of the last moats in software will be network effects

If I build a community based piece of software that has a million users and you build the exact same piece of software and it has 0 users, everyone will buy my software instead

Gaming encapsulates this perfectly. If you build a banger multiplayer game that has millions of players, even if someone copies you and builds the exact same game, you're going to win because of network effects

This is one of those moments. One of those moments where the future is so obvious and so clear.

AI is about to disrupt a multi hundred billion dollar industry and every penny of that will be up for grabs.

i just put Jev inside an open agent harness.

(150x cheaper decision-making than LLM)

agents burn a lot of tokens on decisions that are really just picking one option from a short list, like matching a client request to the right GitHub issue.

so i built a weekly client follow-up agent that does exactly that. i tested it on 40 requests, and it was as accurate as letting Opus make every match, at 150x lower decision cost.

here's the tech stack i used:

→ TrueForge as the agent harness
→ Jev for the matching decisions
→ Daytona as the sandbox for code execution

Jev is a decision model from TypeSafe AI. it takes the options from your app and returns a structured choice with a calibrated confidence score, without generating any text.

that confidence decides what gets a second look. low-confidence matches go back to Opus for review, and in my test, that review caught 5 wrong matches that would otherwise have gone through.

TrueForge is TrueFoundry's harness, and it keeps context small. it loads tool definitions only when needed, writes large tool outputs to files, and lets the agent process data in scripts instead of the conversation.

on DevRev's Enterprise Bench, it solved about as many tasks as Claude Managed Agents on roughly a third of the tokens. it also keeps credentials outside the sandbox and holds every write for approval.

if you want to try this out, TrueForge is fully open source (MIT-licensed) and runs on your own machine with a single command.

TrueForge GitHub: https://t.co/nNsvUzds1A

(don't forget to star 🌟)

2110373001057234970.text:
Two Anthropic engineers built a prompt system that spits out a rigged Blender monster in minutes, and the trick is that it never designs the creature

It designs the skeleton first. Anatomy decides what a creature can do, and everything strange gets added on top of something that works.

> FRAME - limb count, joint positions and weight distribution set before any mesh exists
> FLESH - muscle volumes grown onto that frame, so the silhouette follows the structure
> WARP - the strangeness applied last, as deformation rather than invention

Image-led creature generation looks incredible and falls apart on the rig. Limbs bend in places nothing could bend.

Starting from a skeleton flips the failure. The monster may look wrong on purpose, but it always moves like something alive.

The warp stage is where the personality arrives. Stretch one limb pair, collapse a joint, invert a spine curve, and it reads as a different species.

Because the frame is parametric, every variant is one number away. A hundred monsters cost barely more than the first.

Weight distribution is the detail everyone skips. It decides posture, and posture is what makes a creature look dangerous or sick.

Studios build this knowledge into one senior artist. Here it sits in a prompt that any junior can run.

The full prompt chain and a batch of monsters from one frame are laid out underneath.

Claude Code already has memory.

most people just never run it as a system:

→ write: Opus saves every correction and decision as its own topic file

→ consolidate: an Opus subagent merges, dedupes and prunes them

→ recall: MEMORY.md loads at startup, topic files only when needed

→ the index stays short so nothing gets cut off

Opus remembers. You stop repeating yourself.

paste this into claude code 👇

~/.claude/agents/consolidator.md

---
name: consolidator
description: consolidates auto memory. merges duplicates, prunes stale entries, keeps MEMORY.md a short index.
model: opus
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
---
You maintain this project's auto memory directory.
1. Read MEMORY.md and every topic file.
2. Merge duplicates into one file. Delete facts that are stale or contradicted by newer ones.
3. Rewrite MEMORY.md as an index: one line per memory, linking its topic file.
4. Keep MEMORY.md under 150 lines. Detail lives in topic files, never in the index.
5. Return a short list of what you merged, deleted and kept.
Set up a write, consolidate, recall memory system for this project.
1. Make sure auto memory is on: "autoMemoryEnabled": true in ~/.claude/settings.json. Keep everything else in that file.
2. Create ~/.claude/agents/consolidator.md from the block above.
3. Add to CLAUDE.md: "When I correct you or we make a decision, save it to auto memory as its own topic file. At the end of a long session, run the consolidator agent."

The tech wasn't broken.

The supply chain was.

And for users, that's the same thing.

2110324991594053813.hook: This is getting f*cking useful: Claude can build your app while JEV spots easy jobs that don’t need an expensive AI.
2110324991594053813.text:
This is getting f*cking useful: Claude can build your app while JEV spots easy jobs that don’t need an expensive AI.

Someone packed that setup into an open-source repo called jev-kit.

The idea is simple:

> Claude writes code and solves the hard problems. JEV checks whether the agent picked for a job is more powerful than it needs to be.

> Sending an expensive worker to find a file? The kit can flag it and suggest a cheaper one.

> In enforce mode, it can block dispatches that are 2 or more tiers above what JEV judges necessary.

> It also checks tool calls and sends agents back when they claim they’re done without verifying their work.

There’s an optional browser agent too:

> JEV picks the clicks
> Claude writes text into fields
> Sonnet planner can help with tasks where the steps aren’t clear

That’s the useful part: fewer small decisions left to the big model, with checks around the work it produces.

Start in shadow mode. See what gets flagged before letting it block anything. JEV calls need a TypeSafe API key.

paste this into Claude Code:

“Inspect jonathanavis96/jev-kit. Read docs/install.md and run install/install.sh –check-only.

Show how the tier guard and verification check fit my setup. Keep shadow mode on and show all proposed changes before installing.”

https://t.co/1mnVQdzqlW

Let Claude solve the hard part. Check who you’re paying to do the easy part.

2110440451291402752.text:
whoever leaked this is f*cking crazy

save this for your next agent build.

Jev handles decisions with a fixed set of answers:

> which agent should take this?
> is this lead worth a follow-up?
> does this email need a reply?
> is this source worth reading?
> approve, reject or send to a human?

Claude still does the research, coding and writing.

Jev helps decide which tasks deserve that work.

the useful bit: you can put it BEFORE an expensive step.

before Claude reads 100 documents, screen them for relevance.

before a writing agent drafts 50 replies, check which messages need one.

before a specialist agent starts, check whether a cheaper worker could handle the task.

you stop asking the big model to process everything just to discover half of it needed no action.

here’s a setup worth testing:

> Define the choices. Keep them narrow.
> Give Jev the context it needs to choose.
> Set a confidence threshold in code.
> Send uncertain cases to Claude or a human.
> Log the result and compare it with your old workflow.

Start with 1 decision you repeat constantly.

Email triage. Lead sorting. Document screening etc.

Check missed cases, total cost and time saved. A cheap wrong answer can create expensive cleanup.

Also: if a normal code rule can make the decision, use that first.

> Claude handles the hard work.
> Jev handles the judgment calls you can test.
> Code runs the next step.
> I broke down practical use cases and a router setup in the article below.
> Find the boring decision your agent makes 1,000 times. Start there.

2110109013652193621.text:
THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), docs (pulls the API reference).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before locking a plan, after the same error twice, and before calling a task done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/xb2zLxajd4

save it, you'll use this every single day.

2110588477624717658.name: Aakash Gupta
2110588477624717658.hook: @aakashgupta: Zuckerberg was about to spend up to $200B on an AI that didn't exist yet, so he asked Alexandr Wang if he was sure
2110588477624717658.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was about to spend up to $200 billion, more than the entire Disney company is worth, on an AI that didn't exist yet. So he asked the guy building it if he was sure it would work, and even that guy wasn't sure.

The guy is Alexandr Wang, who runs Meta's AI lab, and the story came out on John Collison's podcast this week. Late last year Meta's top executives were together in Hawaii, and Wang says the CFO, Susan Li, pulled him aside more than once on that trip to warn him that if the model flopped, it would be really, really bad for Meta's finances. All he could show her was his gut read on how the research was going and a few charts.

She had every reason to be nervous. Meta spent $72 billion on capex in 2025, and the plan for 2026 now runs $130 to $145 billion. Last quarter, free cash flow at one of the most profitable companies on the planet fell to $784 million, and Meta borrowed about $25 billion in the bond market in the same stretch.

So why not wait until you know it works?

Because in AI you have to pour the concrete years before you find out what it's for. Meta started planning its two giant clusters, Prometheus in Ohio and the 5 gigawatt Hyperion in Louisiana, back in 2023 and 2024. That was before Llama 4 disappointed, and before Wang ever got the WhatsApp message from Zuck asking if he had time for a call. Meta was building the biggest computers in its history for an AI lab that didn't exist yet.

Wang called the whole thing the opposite of Lean Startup, where you test something small and only spend real money once it works. Muse Wonder got planned in August of last year and shipped this Monday, and the biggest checks were signed with the answer still most of a year away.

What makes it even more nerve-wracking is how few people the bet rides on. Zuck says the research team is under 200 people, closer to 100, with infrastructure staff on top. Run his own numbers and every researcher in that lab is carrying something like a billion dollars of Meta's money.

When John Collison asked whether Meta will actually make money from any of this, Zuck's first answer was "The answer better be yes." A second later he corrected himself and just said yes.

2110594014261162196.name: Aakash Gupta
2110594014261162196.hook: @aakashgupta: a company had an AI interview a candidate, so he sent his own AI clone and walked out
2110594014261162196.text:
A company had an AI interview a guy for a job, so he had his own AI clone sit in for him and walked out of the room.

Which means there's a job interview going on right now with zero people in it. And honestly, he made the most rational move of anybody involved. An economist basically called it back in 1973.

His name was Michael Spence, and he won a Nobel Prize for this idea. Companies can't see inside your head to know if you're any good, so they look at stuff that's a pain for you to produce. You spend four years getting a degree, or you sit on a live call for an hour where you can't hide anything. The hassle is the whole point. Somebody who isn't serious about the job won't put up with it, and that's how the company sorts real candidates from everyone else.

Problem is, AI has been making that stuff easy to fake. Cover letters went first, then résumés. Gartner surveyed 3,000 job seekers and 6% admitted to some kind of interview fraud, like having someone else pretend to be them. Researchers at Palo Alto Networks showed a person with zero editing experience could build a fake candidate good enough to get through a video interview in about 70 minutes.

That left the live interview as pretty much the last thing that still took real effort from you. Then companies decided their own side of it wasn't worth a recruiter's time and started sending avatars.

Put yourself in his shoes for a second. The company wouldn't spend one minute of a human's time on him, but still expected him to sit there and perform for software that turns him into a score. If they're not going to show up, why would he? The company was the first one to skip its own interview, and all he did was return the favor.

So you've got two AIs trading polished answers while his camera films an empty room, and nobody comes out of it knowing anything. The company has no clue if he can actually do the job, and he has no clue if the job is even real. Gartner found only about half of job seekers believe the postings they apply to are legit in the first place.

I'd bet the fix ends up looking pretty old school. Gartner also found 62% of candidates are more likely to apply when a job requires an in-person interview, so the serious ones are already telling companies they'd rather just show up. A lot of companies paid good money to automate the handshake, and they're about to pay again to bring it back.

2110812913347039293.text:
OpenAI just released GPT-Live-1.1 for ChatGPT voice today. Here's what you need to know.

GPT-Live-1.1 is an update to OpenAI's GPT-Live voice model, which launched in July 2026. It brings new voices, better accents and less "checking..." to Voice in ChatGPT, Codex and dots. OpenAI says it rolls out today to all users.

The new voices cover French, German, Hindi, Mexican Spanish, Korean and Japanese. OpenAI staff say the update also improves multilingual support overall. One staff member added that there is one surprise voice not listed in the post.

The "checking..." fix targets a common annoyance. Before, the assistant often said things like "let me check that" every few seconds while waiting on updates. Staff describe the new behavior as more natural preambles and more natural delegation. They also say steerability is improved.

The API is not included yet. OpenAI says GPT-Live-1.1 is coming soon to the API. Staff also say the update brings 13 new voices across Chat, Codex and dots.

Users are split. Some praise the better accents and the reduced pauses. Others say the Chinese voice still has a heavy accent. One user asked whether Hindi voices can handle Hinglish, where speakers switch languages mid-sentence. Another is disappointed that Mexican Spanish is the only Spanish accent added.

Key numbers:
- 13 new voices across ChatGPT, Codex and dots
- 6 languages with new voices: French, German, Hindi, Mexican Spanish, Korean, Japanese
- 3 products getting the update: Voice in ChatGPT, Codex, dots
- Original GPT-Live launched July 2026, with API pricing of $0.05 per minute for GPT-Live-1

GPT-Live-1.1 is rolling out now to all users, with API access still to come.

A big studio wired Opus 5.5 straight into Blender, and the first thing it changed was not modelling at all

Productions do not lose weeks to building assets. They lose them to versions, naming, and files that no longer match the shot list.

> AUDIT - every scene file read and matched against the shot it is supposed to serve
> NAME - objects, collections and materials renamed to the studio’s own convention
> LINK - duplicated assets collapsed into one linked source across the whole project
> CHECK - any scene drifting from the approved version flagged before it reaches render

A hundred artists working in parallel produce a hundred slightly different versions of the same prop.

Nobody notices until the render farm bills for three days of frames built on an outdated asset.

The linking pass is the expensive save. One source, every scene updated at once, no manual chase across departments.

Naming sounds trivial right up until a pipeline script fails because one file was saved under a name nobody else uses.

The model touches no creative decision. Lighting, composition and design stay exactly where the artists left them.

It cleans the part of the job nobody wants and everybody pays for, on every project, at every studio.

The audit pass, the naming rules and a full project cleanup are laid out underneath.

2111164776709521547.text:
Anthropic team built a prompt system that renders finished animation with Fable 5.1, replacing a thirty-person pipeline

Modelling was never the bottleneck. The bottleneck is everyone a shot has to pass through before it is allowed to render.

> BUILD - geometry, rig, materials and lighting produced as one consistent set, no handoffs
> MOVE - animation authored against the rig’s real limits, so nothing has to be fixed later
> CHECK - every frame validated against the shot brief before anything reaches the farm

A traditional pipeline is a relay. Model, rig, animate, light, render, composite, each stage waiting on the one before it.

Most of the time is spent in the gaps. A rig arrives wrong, animation sends it back, and two days vanish.

Collapsing the stages removes the gaps entirely. The rig cannot arrive wrong, because the same pass that built it is using it.

The validation step is what makes it shippable. A frame that misses the brief never costs farm hours.

None of this makes creative choices. Someone still decides what the shot is; the system only stops it being a scheduling problem.

Thirty people were never doing thirty jobs. They were doing one job and handing it to each other.

The full prompt chain and a finished shot rendered end to end are laid out underneath.

2111338922735554709.name: Aakash Gupta
2111338922735554709.hook: @aakashgupta: OpenAI tells federal judges there may soon be no scientific way to tell real video from fake
2111338922735554709.text:
OpenAI just told federal judges there may soon be no scientific way to tell a real video from a fake. So the guy your doorbell cam caught stealing your packages can stand up in court and say "that's AI." Only 15 of 931 federal judges surveyed have had someone try that.

That number is going to go up fast. Two law professors, Bobby Chesney and Danielle Citron, saw this coming back in 2018 and called it the liar's dividend. Once everybody knows a perfect fake is possible, real footage stops ending the argument, and a jury that hears "could be AI" suddenly has something to chew on.

And detection was always going to lose this fight. The first image generators that actually worked, GANs back in 2014, got good by training a forger against a detective over and over until the detective couldn't catch it anymore. So any detector somebody publishes basically becomes practice for the next model. Meta's product director told the same panel that regular people already can't tell recent AI video from the real thing, and making it costs next to nothing.

Now think about what the judges have spent three years drafting. Under a draft rule called 901(c), if you want to call an exhibit fake, you first have to bring some evidence it was fabricated, and then the other side has to prove it's real. Both of those steps assume somebody can actually run a test, which is the exact thing OpenAI just told them might never exist.

So courts are going to lean on people again, kind of like before anyone owned a camera. It'll come down to who shot the video and whether they're willing to swear to it.

The tech industry's best idea is to stamp footage the second it's recorded so anything without a stamp looks suspicious. Every photo from a Pixel 10's camera app already gets a cryptographic signature baked in, and Google's camera lead said the whole point is getting people suspicious of pictures that show up without one. But OpenAI's lawyer also told the judges that every company runs its own system and nothing reads all of them. A stamp only helps if the camera that shot the video added one in the first place, and your doorbell probably didn't.

Until that changes, every real video of somebody doing something awful comes with a free alibi.

This is f*cking insane.

Chinese researchers just dropped a paper with a title that will make every agent framework nervous: "The End of Harness Engineering".

The argument fits in one line: writing the program around the model is finished as a skill.

A harness written by a human is one person's guess about one task on one afternoon. It ships, nobody re-reads it, nobody scores it, and the agent runs that guess for months.

A harness written by the loop is a file that grades itself. A small 4B model reads what failed, writes 8 edits, and only the edit that scores best on held-out questions survives.

The big model never changes. The file around it does, every round.

So the human job collapses to one artifact: the scoring set. You write the questions, never the program.

Frameworks turn disposable. The exam turns into the job.

That is the exact loop I built and documented below: one https://t.co/JlQQhqH44N, 300 Kimi K3 workers, 37 rewrites in 41 rounds, zero opened by me.

The whole paper in one line: write the exam before the code ↓

Nothing about the drawings looked different. What changed is that the model knows a building has to be assembled, not just drawn.

> DRAFT - the structure modelled from the brief with real materials and real spans
> CLASH - every system checked against the others before anything reaches a drawing set
> CODE - clearances, egress and loads validated against the rules that apply to the site
> BUILD - the sequence checked, so nothing is designed in a place it cannot be installed

Clash detection already exists. It runs at the end, which is exactly when a conflict is most expensive to resolve.

Here it runs while the geometry is still soft. A pipe crossing a beam gets moved before anyone has drawn the beam’s details.

The sequencing check is the one nobody automates. A perfect design can still be impossible to assemble in order.

Code compliance is where hand-drafting quietly leaks time. One missed clearance sends a full set back weeks.

The model does not design the building. It catches the conflicts a person only finds after the drawings are finished.

Review cycles went from several rounds to barely more than one, and that is the whole saving.

2111379227278758394.text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: let Opus 5.5 write the plan as a script, and let 12 cheap agents run it while Opus sits idle at zero tokens.

Same task, two ways: Opus solo was 49% done and still running. The swarm finished in 9 minutes on 165k tokens.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --swarm haiku,sonnet

here's the split:

→ Opus 5.5 writes plan.js, then stops reading anything
→ 6 Haiku 5.5 agents audit every file in parallel
→ 4 Sonnet 5.5 agents patch each fix in its own isolated copy
→ 2 Haiku 5.5 agents cross-check, 8 of 9 findings survive
Opus only shows up at two moments:
→ writing the plan before the run
→ signing off on the verified fixes after it
Opus plans. Haiku scans. Sonnet ships.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 3,767 forks this run - which model, which lane, retry or stop - resolved in code, and only the genuinely split ones ever reach Opus

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the main session on xhigh and writes plan.js
> scan audits each file on Haiku 5.5, six in parallel
> patch applies each fix on Sonnet 5.5 in its own isolated copy
> verify cross-checks every finding on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 reads only what survived, then signs off
> JEV resolves micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

Run the main session on Opus 5.5 with effort xhigh and swarm haiku,sonnet.
Have Opus write the plan as a script: scan on Haiku 5.5, patch on Sonnet 5.5 in isolated copies, verify on Haiku 5.5.
Let the phases overlap - each finding moves on as soon as its own stage finishes, no waiting for the batch.
Never surface raw agent output to the main session, only verified results.
Route deterministic forks (model choice, lane choice, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

Boris Cherny, at YC: "Every six months, completely clear out your CLAUDE.md, strip away your custom skills, and remove your hooks. Let the model run fresh and you might be amazed by what happens"

The logic behind it:

Your previous prompt rules were written to cover up flaws in older system versions

Fresh model releases no longer suffer from those exact limitations

Keeping those legacy prompts around might actually degrade Claude's output quality today

The step by step process:

1. Erase CLAUDE.md, along with all integrated skills and hooks
2. Go about your normal workflow and spot where the AI starts to drift off course
3. Bring back a single rule only when you notice a specific error recurring over and over
4. Execute this reset whenever a major model upgrade drops

Things to keep:

Essential safety protocols and strict compliance guidelines

Non-obvious project quirks that cannot be inferred directly from reading code

Things to trash:

Directory layouts, lists of packages, and high-level architecture breakdowns

Any information the AI can figure out on its own by analyzing your codebase

scale the verifier before the workers, or the fleet eats its own output

6. demand independent evidence (a diff, a log, a rendered artifact) before anything is marked done
humans sign off only on irreversible or ambiguous moves

the result: a chatbot turns into a 24/7 operating system
every task owned, every handoff typed, every result proven
