2111545985835127102.text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: Opus 5.5 stops typing and becomes the brain. It plans, answers questions, reviews the diff, and nothing else.

Same feature, two ways: Opus solo was 49% done at the 12 minute mark. The brain plus swarm finished the whole thing at 11:50.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --brain --swarm haiku,sonnet

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 breaks dark mode into 16 tasks and assigns a model to each one
→ 12 Haiku 5.5 agents take the simple files, 4 Sonnet 5.5 agents take the hard ones
→ 8 slots run in parallel, agents ask the brain when they get stuck
→ the brain answers in 0.6s and is busy only 22% of the run

the part most setups get wrong: the big model reads every agent transcript and becomes the bottleneck.

here the brain reads one diff, not 16 chats. it thinks in short bursts while 8 hands keep moving.

three questions came back mid-run: contrast AA or AAA, which palette the chart uses in dark, dark mode in emails. the brain answered two and cut the third as out of scope.

15 of 16 tasks shipped. one got killed by the brain before anyone wasted time on it.

Opus thinks. Haiku and Sonnet type. Nobody waits.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 5,709 forks this run - which model, retry or stop, ask the brain or not - resolved in code, and only the genuinely split ones ever reach Opus

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs as the brain on xhigh, plans the tasks and assigns models
> 12 simple tasks go to Haiku 5.5, 4 hard ones go to Sonnet 5.5
> 8 slots run in parallel, agents ask the brain only when a fork is split
> the brain answers in under a second and never reads raw agent output
> Opus 5.5 reviews one merged diff and approves or cuts tasks
> JEV resolves micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
Run the main session as a brain on Opus 5.5 with effort xhigh and swarm haiku,sonnet.
The brain plans, assigns a model per task, answers agent questions and reviews the final diff. It never writes code itself.
Route simple tasks to Haiku 5.5 and hard ones to Sonnet 5.5, 8 slots in parallel.
The brain reads one merged diff, never raw agent transcripts.
Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: the brain is allowed to cut any task as out of scope before it is built.
Route deterministic forks (model choice, retries, whether to ask the brain) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ 
https://t.co/GoHZ0pp10F

save it, it'll come in handy.

2111444869956739293.name: The Greatest
2111444869956739293.hook: Honestly I couldn't f*ckin believe it actually happened
2111444869956739293.text:
Honestly I couldn't f*ckin believe it actually happened 

Stanford data research team just leaked the secret way they process data

your coding pipeline is waiting 2 seconds per row for a model to say "refund" or "bug"

that's what happens when you send a frontier LLM to label a table. it reads, it thinks, it writes a paragraph, and you parse one word out of it.

They stopped doing that. They use Jev.

Jev doesn't write. it picks from the labels you gave it, returns a probability, and moves to the next row.

someone benchmarked it on 500 examples from Stanford's SST-2 dataset against Claude Sonnet 5:

-> accuracy: 95.4% vs 95.6%
-> median latency: 376 ms vs 2,076 ms
-> throughput: 18.2 rows/s vs 3.5 rows/s
-> cost per 1,000 rows: $0.015 vs $0.80

same answer quality. ~5x faster. ~50x cheaper.

and it runs where your data already lives:

-> jev4pg: 41 Jev operators inside PostgreSQL. filter, extract, rank and match rows in SQL, with parallel execution and repeated values sharing one judgment
https://t.co/uCm6kRacEX

-> duckdb-jev: a native DuckDB extension that packs up to 1,000 judgments into one request and streams them straight from a query
https://t.co/W4MrKZktBm

-> jevframe: a .jev accessor for pandas and Polars. ask a question about every row, get a normal column back
https://t.co/qlJxFaQNCl

the database still does the math. Jev only takes the part where something has to be understood.

the catch: it's not magic on every dataset. on 4-topic news it scored 84% vs Claude's 90%, and a fine-tuned BERT beat both. measure it on your own data first.

> let SQL do the joins.
> let Jev do the judgment.
> let the frontier model handle what's actually hard.

bookmark this before your next labeling job eats a weekend to process.

2111709866872160283.name: Aakash Gupta
2111709866872160283.hook: @aakashgupta: someone broke into OpenCode and grabbed developers' OpenAI/Claude/Google API keys
2111709866872160283.text:
A bunch of developers woke up this morning to AI charges they never made. Somebody broke into OpenCode, a popular AI coding app, and grabbed the keys people use to pay for OpenAI, Claude and Google. The company says the whole thing was part of a large scale operation to copy the AI models themselves.

The timing is what got me. Five days earlier, Anthropic put out a post saying it had cut the amount of data these copycats could pull out of Claude by 90 to 99%.

Here's how the copying works, because everything else hinges on it. You hit a top model like Claude or GPT with millions of questions, save every answer and especially the step-by-step reasoning, and train your own cheaper model to imitate it. The industry calls it distillation. Back in February, Anthropic said DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax had done this more than 16 million times through about 24,000 fake accounts, and one proxy network was running over 20,000 of those accounts at once.

So the labs started going after the fake accounts. Anthropic built a classifier that spots people fishing for Claude's reasoning, and it bans the accounts doing it, a lot of the time within two hours. It says tens of thousands have been banned so far.

Once fake accounts get that easy to catch, a real one becomes the most valuable thing a copycat can get their hands on. A real developer's key comes with a verified owner and months of normal usage behind it, so the traffic blends right in, and the developer is the one who gets the bill.

There's also a line in Anthropic's own post that makes older keys worth even more. Its newest models have a protection called preserved thinking, which stops people from editing Claude's earlier reasoning to trick more of it out, and it only applies to API accounts created on or after August 31 this year. Somebody who signed up in the spring is still on the old rules. To be fair, OpenCode hasn't said which models the stolen keys hit or how they were used, so nobody's shown these attackers went through that door. Anyone shopping for stolen keys can read the same blog post, though.

And look at who gets stuck with the penalties. Since late September, Anthropic charges for requests its classifier blocks, and accounts caught distilling get their limits tightened and then get banned. All of that lands on the account, and the account belongs to whoever pasted their key into the tool. One developer said his OpenAI, Anthropic and Google spend alerts all went off before he went to bed, and Google was the only one that shut things down on its own. The keys came out of an old system OpenCode was in the middle of shutting down.

The better the labs get at catching fake accounts, the more your old API key sitting in some app is worth to somebody else.

This is f*cking gold..

Chinese researchers just published a paper that kills the hottest skill of the year: "The End of Context Engineering".

The argument fits in one line: a context window packed by a human is a guess made before the model has looked.

You pack what you would have needed. The model needs something else. Too much of the obvious, none of the surprising.

So the paper hands the model an index instead: one line per thing that exists, never the content. The model names what it needs, pulls only that, runs the task, and every item gets credited or blamed for the result.

What did not move the score gets dropped. What did gets pinned for the next task.

Across 300 tasks: score 0.14 higher than the hand-built pipeline with a window 81% smaller.

Three hundred prompts cannot be packed by hand. They can be scored by a loop.

So you stop being the person who decides what the model sees. You become the person who names what exists and reads the score.

Pipelines turn disposable. The index turns into the job.

That is the exact system I run and documented below: one index file, 300 Kimi K3 tasks, 212 items pinned, 4,970 dropped, zero prompts packed by me.

The whole paper in one line: index the shelf, not the page ↓

2111814751843983552.text:
Anthropic turned a model loose on sequencing data nobody could classify and pulled out a virus that matches nothing on record

It was never looking for a virus. The question was what the leftovers are - the reads every pipeline throws away as junk.

> KEEP - the unclassified fraction of each dataset retained instead of discarded
> SHAPE - those reads assembled by structure, with no reference genome to lean on
> HOST - each assembly matched to what else was living in the same sample

Every sequencing run produces a pile that matches nothing. Standard practice is to delete it and move on.

That pile is not noise. It is mostly things with no close relative in any database, which is the definition of undiscovered.

Assembling without a reference is the hard part. You cannot align to something known when nothing known is close.

The host step is what makes it useful. A sequence alone says little; a sequence plus what it was living inside says a lot.

Most of the biosphere has never been catalogued, and the evidence has been sitting in discarded data for years.

The assembly method and what the samples contained are laid out underneath.

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: stop treating Claude like one worker. Make Opus 5.5 a commander and give it 12 agents in 4 squads.

Same release, two ways: Opus alone was 2% through on one thread. The command center shipped the whole v2.0 in 2 minutes on 12 threads.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --command-center 12 "ship v2.0"

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 turns "ship v2.0" into 12 tasks across 4 squads
→ CODE and OPS squads run on Sonnet 5.5, TEST and DOCS on Haiku 5.5
→ every agent reports back in one line, never raw logs
→ Opus only wakes up when something breaks or needs approval

the part most people get wrong: the commander watches everything.

read 12 agent transcripts and your expensive model becomes the slowest part of the room.

here the commander stays at 8k of context the entire run. it plans, it waits, it reads 12 one-line reports, it opens the release gate.

REA sits underneath on anything legacy: before a squad touches old code, REA reverse-engineers it into a spec, so agents build from the spec and never from 500 files nobody understands.

Opus commands. Sonnet builds. Haiku checks. REA explains the old code.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which squad, which model, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the commander only sees the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs as commander, splits the mission into tasks and squads
> CODE squad on Sonnet 5.5 writes endpoints, refactors auth, migrates the db
> TEST squad on Haiku 5.5 runs unit, e2e and load tests
> DOCS squad on Haiku 5.5 writes changelog, api docs and release notes

OPS squad on Sonnet 5.5 handles staging, health checks and canary rollout

REA reverse-engineers any legacy module into a spec before a squad touches it

every agent reports one line, the commander never reads raw output

Opus 5.5 holds the release gate and waits for all 12 reports

JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

2112126341516603512.text:
OpenAI’s studio integration lands in Blender this month, and the interesting part is that it refuses to generate anything twice

Most tools race to produce assets. This one spends its first pass deciding what already exists and should never be made again.

> INDEX - the studio’s entire asset library read and described, not just filenamed
> MATCH - every new request checked against that index before a single polygon is made
> REUSE - a close enough match returned as a link to the original, not as a copy
> ADAPT - near misses modified from the existing asset instead of built from nothing
> MAKE - only genuinely new requests sent to generation
> FILE - whatever is produced indexed immediately, so the next request can find it

Studios already own most of what they keep rebuilding. They just cannot find it.

A library with ten thousand assets and no semantic index is the same as an empty one. Nobody searches it, so everyone remodels.

Generative tools made that worse. Producing a new chair became faster than locating the three chairs already on disk.

The adapt step is the quiet win. A modified existing asset inherits its materials, its scale and its pipeline history.

Every reuse also keeps the library coherent, instead of filling it with near-duplicates nobody can tell apart.

The index format, the match threshold and a full reuse log are laid out underneath.

This is f*cking insane.

Chinese researchers just dropped "The End of Loop Engineering" four months after the term was invented. Fastest death of a discipline I've seen.

The claim in one sentence: the run is the only thing that knows when it is finished.

Every loop you have ever written had a cap, a budget and an exit condition decided before the first action. The paper calls all three the same mistake.

What replaces them is almost nothing: a verifier the agent cannot fool (tests, compiler, diff) and a memory of its last three states.

> Verifier passes -> done, no extra iteration.
> Three identical states -> hand it to a human with the full trace.
> Anything else -> act again.

Across 2,400 runs that ended at the wrong moment 4% as often as a fixed cap, with 2,391 self-stops and 9 escalations.

So the loop engineer leaves and one script stays: the check that says the work is done. You write that. The agent writes the ending.

Loop engineering turns disposable. The check turns into the job.

That is exactly what I run and documented below: one verifier, 300 Kimi K3 workers, zero caps written by me.

One line to remember: the exit is observed, never authored ↓

THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: you stop writing agent configs by hand. One prompt, and Opus 5.5 writes the entire swarm for you.

By hand that is 16 prompts, 16 tool configs, 16 test harnesses and 2,312 lines you type yourself. Here you type one line.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus "build REA swarm ×16 for legacy/"

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 reads 578 files and splits them into 16 services
→ it writes 16 specs in parallel, 1,037 lines, no templates
→ every spec becomes one REA agent, one reverse-engineer per service
→ each agent gets tested as it lands, 3/48 checks already green at 3 minutes

the part everyone gets wrong: they hand-write every agent and then wonder why 16 of them drift apart.

here one architect writes all 16 specs from the same read of the codebase, so every agent is wired the same way and nothing gets forgotten.

REA is the piece doing the real work underneath: each agent reverse-engineers its own service, dry-runs on three files first, then writes its spec from what it actually found, not from what you guessed.

you wrote 1 line. Opus wrote 1,037.

Opus architects. REA reverse-engineers. The swarm builds itself.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which service, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the architect only sees the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs as architect, reads the repo and splits it into services
> it writes one spec per service, all 16 in parallel, from a single read
> every spec spawns one REA agent that reverse-engineers that service
> each agent dry-runs on a few files before writing anything
> specs get tested as they land, the architect monitors all 16 in flight
> Opus 5.5 deploys once every spec is ready
JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 as an architect that writes agent specs, never agent code by hand.
2. Point it at a repo, let it split the repo into services and write one spec per service, all in parallel from a single read.
3. Every spec spawns one REA agent that reverse-engineers its own service and dry-runs on a few files before writing anything.
4. Test each spec as it lands, never wait for all of them to finish first.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: no agent ships until its spec passes its own checks.
6. Route deterministic forks (service choice, tool choice, retries) through JEV.

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳

2112412243594019016.text:
Claude Code has a built-in research mode that fact-checks itself before it answers.

/deep-research [your question]

It sends agents to search from several angles, pulls the sources, cross-checks them against each other, votes on every claim and gives you one cited report. Claims that don't survive the cross-check get dropped.

Want that for any task? Start your prompt with "ultracode:" and Claude writes a workflow that runs many agents in parallel instead of working one step at a time.

Prompts that work, from Anthropic's docs:

ultracode: audit every API endpoint under src/routes/ for missing auth checks, and adversarially verify each finding before reporting it

use a workflow to run npx tsc --noEmit and keep fixing the errors until the type check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress

use a workflow to find flaky tests: run the suite repeatedly and stop once two rounds in a row find nothing new

use a workflow to research how our three competitors handle rate limiting, read their docs and changelogs in parallel, then compare the approaches

Type /workflows to watch every agent live, and press s to save a run as your own command.

Works on all paid plans. On Pro, turn on Dynamic workflows in /config first. Workflows use more tokens, so try one folder before the whole repo.

SAVE THIS: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google have all released AI tools that hunt security bugs in your code. Here's each one and how to run it.

A team of agents maps your app, builds a threat model, hunts through every component and checks each finding independently. It can turn confirmed bugs into patch files.
/plugin install claude-security@claude-plugins-official
Then type /claude-security

Scans a whole repo, one folder or just your latest changes, validates what it finds, writes patches and drafts a SECURITY.md.
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
cs scan .

3. Security Audit Skill by Cloudflare (31K stars)
Six phases, and every finding is rechecked by a fresh agent that didn't find it. Works in most coding agents.
npx skills add https://t.co/ptOfJggqQB --skill security-audit
Then ask: "security audit this codebase"

4. Mantis by Google (2.5K stars)
Builds a threat model, tries to reproduce each bug, then patches it and attacks the fix to prove it holds. Google says to run it only in an isolated environment.
https://t.co/36azMYVvEz

Run at least one before you ship anything that handles user data.

Opus 5.5 inside Blender costs $4 per million input tokens, and it just beat a stack of specialist tools that charge by the seat

Price per seat hides the real comparison. One is a subscription per person, the other is a bill that scales with what you actually make.

> ASSET - a full set of product models built from one brief, geometry and materials included
> SHOT - the same products staged, lit and rendered across a dozen backgrounds
> COST - every tool’s output priced against what the run actually consumed

Photoroom and the rest are built around a photo. They cut, relight and restage something that already exists.

That ceiling shows up fast. No photo means no output, and a product that is not built yet has no photo at all.

Opus 5.5 starts earlier. The model is built in Blender, so every angle, every material and every background is a render away.

At $4 in and $20 out per million tokens, a full catalogue costs less than one seat of the specialist tools per month.

The quality gap is not subtle either. Real geometry holds up under lighting changes in a way a cut-out never does.

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: stop asking for an answer. Give it a stop condition and let one agent loop until it hits it.

Same codebase, two ways: one-shot got 61% and guessed the rest. The loop ran 43 times and came back with 388 of 388 rules verified.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus --loop "map legacy/ until 100% verified"

here's the split:
→ you write one prompt and then do nothing, zero edits for the entire run
→ REA loops read → extract → verify → fix on its own
→ every rule it extracts gets replayed against real prod logs before it counts
→ the loop only stops when all 388 rules pass, not when the model feels done
the part everyone gets wrong: they accept the first pass.
a single pass over 16 services gives you a confident document where most of it was never checked against anything.
here rules.md grows every loop. 388 rules across auth, billing, payments, checkout, admin and the rest, each one marked verified only after it survives a replay.

three rules came back wrong. the agent re-read the source, fixed them, and looped again instead of shipping them.

one prompt from you, 43 loops from it, 0 edits by you.

Opus drives. REA reads and verifies. The loop decides when it is done.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file next, re-loop or stop, retry or fail) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the model only sees the ones that actually split

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the session with a stop condition, not a task
> REA loops read, extract, verify and fix on every pass
> every extracted rule is replayed against prod logs before it counts as verified
> any mismatch sends that module back for a re-read instead of shipping
> rules.md grows each loop until the stop condition is met
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 and give every long task a stop condition, never a single pass.
2. Loop read, extract, verify and fix until the condition is met.
3. Every extracted rule must be replayed against real logs or tests before it counts as verified.
4. Any mismatch triggers a re-read of that module, never a patched guess.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: unverified findings are never written into the final document.
6. Route deterministic forks (next file, re-loop or stop, retries) through JEV.

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ 
https://t.co/GoHZ0potb7

save it, you'll use this on every legacy repo from now on.

This is absolutely f*cking insane.

A Stanford AI research group combines JEV with Claude Code to sort 78+ billion data points every 12 minutes.

so the trick is stupidly simple:

Jev runs a cheap first pass on everything. Claude only gets the hard cases.

instead of:

all data -> Claude -> $$$

it's:

all data -> Jev -> only the unsure ones -> Claude

and here's the part people miss. every Jev answer comes with a probability. that's your filter:

-> Jev is 90%+ sure? keep the answer, done
-> below that? send it up to Claude

you set the cutoff once. the boring stuff never touches the expensive model.

where this pays off right away:

-> tagging support tickets
-> sorting your inbox
-> filtering leads
-> cleaning a messy spreadsheet
-> moderating comments

faster. cheaper. way less compute and tokens burned.

Jev sorts the mail so the genius only opens what matters.

LLMs think. Jev decides. code does the job.

2112516279617945940.name: cedric
2112516279617945940.hook: @cedric_chee: OpenAI quietly renamed 'GPT-6 Pro' to 'GPT-6 Astra Pro' - what Pro mode actually is
2112516279617945940.text:
OpenAI got its own Pro reasoning mode wrong. They quietly corrected "GPT-6 Pro" to "GPT-6 Astra Pro". I spent yesterday digging through this confusing mess. fml.

What I figured out:
- GPT-6 Pro is powered by Astra, but Pro isn't simply another reasoning-effort level above Max.
- Pro is a reasoning mode, separate from reasoning effort (thinking level).
- ChatGPT's Pro selection switches model families. Instant through xhigh use GPT-6 Sol, while Pro uses GPT-6 Astra.
- Standard vs. Pro mode: Different execution configurations, not just different thinking budgets.
- Pro isn't necessarily better than Astra Max/Ultra on every task.
- Is Pro equivalent to Ultra thinking? No.
And don't confuse Ultra with Ultrafast.
- Many people assume Pro is just the same model thinking for much longer. That's incomplete.
- I'm already using Astra in Codex and Work. What GPT-6 Astra Pro adds in Chat is a different execution configuration and experience.

Pro can involve additional inference-time compute and orchestration, including parallel agents, rather than simply extending sequential reasoning. The exact reasoning budgets, agent counts, and aggregation mechanisms aren't disclosed. (why?)

Basically, extended thinking from the dinosaur era, now with orchestration ig.

From my testing:
ChatGPT Chat Pro use Astra with undisclosed reasoning effort and parallel agents. I've observed ~3 subagents working for roughly an hour for critical planning/spec (product design, sys arch), big discovery, and high-stakes work where mistakes have serious consequences. I can see the value. For basic research, Pro mode is overkill.

2112761797975679099.name: Aakash Gupta
2112761797975679099.hook: @aakashgupta: Anthropic's draft IPO filing shows $80.7B loss in six months, ~$72B from rising valuation
2112761797975679099.text:
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, lost $80.7 billion in six months, according to its draft IPO filing. About $72 billion of that happened because the company got more valuable, and if its value had crashed instead, the same accounting rule would have booked it a gain on paper.

That sounds made up, so here's how it works.

When Anthropic raised money, a lot of it came in through convertible notes and similar deals. Think of them as IOUs that turn into stock later. Accounting rules make the company list those IOUs as something it owes, and price them at whatever that future stock is worth today.

Anthropic started 2026 valued at around $350 billion. It raised at $380 billion in February, and by late May it closed a $65 billion round at $965 billion, passing OpenAI. Every jump made those IOUs worth more on paper, and every time that happened the books recorded it as a loss, even though no actual cash went anywhere.

The same thing happened last year. Anthropic's 2025 net loss was $42 billion, and more than $34 billion of it came from this exact kind of adjustment, in a year when its value went from $61.5 billion in March to $350 billion by November.

Take the $72 billion out and you're left with a loss of about $8.7 billion over six months, on $16.3 billion of revenue. A year earlier, first-half revenue was $1.1 billion. Then Q3 by itself brought in $16.8 billion, more than the whole first half, and Anthropic told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis that quarter.

The number I'd actually watch is somewhere else in the filing. Anthropic said it could spend as much as $750 billion on computing power over the next few years, and two customers made up about a fifth of its 2026 revenue. At last week's investor event, people reportedly talked about a valuation around $1.5 trillion, down from the roughly $2 trillion that was floating around for the November IPO.

Anthropic's IPO is going to come down to whether revenue growing 45% a quarter can keep up with a $750 billion computing bill.

2112946824327709087.name: wast3
2112946824327709087.hook: Anthropic engineering team stopped letting models touch the app and gave them a script layer instead, and the whole thing got faster overnight
2112946824327709087.text:
Anthropic engineering team stopped letting models touch the app and gave them a script layer instead, and the whole thing got faster overnight

A model holding the tool directly has to understand the tool. A model writing a script only has to understand the job.

> READ - the task parsed once into what has to change, never into UI steps
> WRITE - the model emits a script instead of clicking through an interface
> RUN - the script executes natively, at the speed the software actually works
> CHECK - the result verified against the task, not against what the model intended
> KEEP - scripts that worked saved, so the same job never gets re-reasoned

Direct tool use looks impressive and runs slowly. Every action is a round trip: look, decide, act, look again.

A script collapses all of that into one pass. The thinking happens once, the execution happens at machine speed.

The keep step is where it compounds. The second time a job appears, there is nothing to generate at all.

Verification against the task matters more than it sounds. A script that runs cleanly can still do the wrong thing confidently.

Most agent stacks are slow for this exact reason. Not weak models, just models forced to operate software one click at a time.

The script layer, the verification rules and a full before-and-after run are laid out underneath.

2113212224529461751.hook: Gemini 3.1 Pro landed in Blender, and the first thing it does is watch the viewport instead of reading the scene file
2113212224529461751.text:
Gemini 3.1 Pro landed in Blender, and the first thing it does is watch the viewport instead of reading the scene file

Every other integration works from the data. This one works from what the render actually shows, which is the only thing a client ever sees.

> LOOK - the viewport sampled as an image, the same way a human judges a shot
> READ - the scene graph pulled in alongside it, so geometry and appearance are compared
> SPOT - anything that looks wrong on screen but reads as correct in the data flagged
> FIX - the underlying nodes and transforms edited, never the image

A scene can be technically perfect and still look broken. Wrong normals, bad scale, a material that reads as plastic under one light.

None of that shows up in the file. The data says everything is fine, because by its own rules it is.

Comparing the two is the whole trick. The gap between what the scene says and what the frame shows is where every real bug lives.

Fixing at the node level keeps it clean. Nothing is painted over, so the next render inherits the actual correction.

Most artists already work this way - look, judge, go back and fix. This just closes that loop without a person in it.

The viewport pass, the comparison rules and a full fix log are laid out underneath.

2113207736146043268.text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: keep one expensive brain and make everything else cheap. Opus 5.5 thinks, Haiku 5.5 does the grunt work, and your bill drops 79%.

Same task, two ways: all-Opus would have cost $1.13. This run cost $0.23.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus    # agents: model: haiku

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 plans, decides and reviews, and burns 40k tokens for $0.21
→ 12 Haiku 5.5 agents fan out across read, grep and test lanes
→ those 12 agents chew through 180k tokens for $0.02
→ Opus never reads raw agent output, only 3 summaries at 6k tokens

the part most people get wrong: they let the expensive model do the reading.

Haiku is 40x cheaper per token. mapping 48 files cost $0.009. doing that on Opus is where the whole budget goes.

one catch worth knowing: past 100k of context Haiku jumps to 5x its own price, so every agent is kept under 100k on purpose.

that is the whole design. the brain stays small and expensive, the hands stay huge and cheap, and nothing raw ever crosses between them.

Opus plans. Haiku reads. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 1,301 forks this run - which file, which agent, retry or stop - resolved in code at 0.90 sharpness, and only the split ones (0.48 on "which agent") ever reach Opus

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the main session, plans the lanes and decides what happens next
> 12 Haiku 5.5 agents fan out across read, grep and test, each kept under 100k context
> every agent returns a summary, never raw files or logs
> Opus 5.5 reads 3 summaries at 6k tokens and reviews the result
> JEV resolves 1,301 micro-forks in code and escalates only the split ones

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 for planning, decisions and review only.
2. Set every subagent to Haiku 5.5 and fan the grunt work out across read, grep and test lanes.
3. Keep each agent under 100k of context, split the work further if it goes over.
4. Agents return summaries only, raw files and logs never enter the main session.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: if a task is reading, searching or running tests, it never runs on Opus.

Route deterministic forks (file choice, agent choice, retries) through JEV.

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/GoHZ0potb7

save it, it'll come in handy.

2113193983811748181.text:
I GAVE CLAUDE CODE AND CODEX THE SAME MEMORY

All agents start every new session as brilliant strangers. They don’t know what changed since the last conversation and they can’t pick up where another agent left off. You end up re-briefing, pasting giant handoff prompts, and burning tokens on context they already had.

I’ve been running a different setup with @FulcraDynamics 

→ Claude Code works on the repo, discovers the important decisions, progress and next steps  
→ Before the session ends it writes that context into a shared workspace (files + records)  
→ I open a fresh Codex session  
→ Codex reads the same context and continues exactly where Claude stopped  

No copy-pasting. No “here’s everything we did before”. The second agent just picks it up.

The context isn’t locked inside Claude or Codex. It’s mine. I decide which agent (or which person) sees what. Shared memory across tools and vendors, handoffs without friction, permissioned so nothing extra is exposed.

Fulcra is the durable context layer underneath: real-world data, agent work, files and records normalized on a timeline. Agents query what changed since last time and only pull what they need. First 5 GB free. Your data stays encrypted, exportable and deletable.

This is the closest I’ve gotten to making multiple coding agents actually feel like one team instead of a bunch of strangers that restart cold every time

How to become an LLM Engineer from scratch in 6 months.

100% free resources.

No degree required.

Here's the exact roadmap, month by month.

Bookmark this. You'll come back to it.

MONTH 1: Foundations

Learn:
→ Python until it feels boring
→ the math intuition behind neural nets (vectors, gradients, probability)
→ how models learn from data

Resources:
→ https://t.co/9rJ3kXnLVM Practical Deep Learning
→ 3Blue1Brown's neural networks series on YouTube

Build:
→ an image classifier you trained yourself

Checkpoint: you can explain what a gradient does without googling.

MONTH 2: Neural nets and transformers

Learn:
→ backpropagation from scratch
→ tokenization
→ attention and the transformer architecture

Resources:
→ Andrej Karpathy's Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
→ start with micrograd, finish with building GPT

Build:
→ a tiny GPT trained on text you choose

Checkpoint: you can draw a transformer block from memory.

MONTH 3: Build an LLM yourself

Learn:
→ pretraining
→ data pipelines
→ how training scales with data and compute

Resources:
→ Sebastian Raschka's Build an LLM From Scratch (all code free on GitHub)
→ Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch (free lectures)

Build:
→ your own small language model, trained end to end

Checkpoint: you know why every line of your training loop exists.

MONTH 4: Fine tuning

Learn:
→ supervised fine tuning
→ LoRA and other efficient methods
→ preference training basics

Resources:
→ Hugging Face LLM Course

Build:
→ fine tune an open model on one narrow task
→ measure it against the base model

Checkpoint: you can prove your model got better, with numbers.

MONTH 5: Prompting, tools, RAG and agents

Learn:
→ prompt engineering that actually holds up
→ tool use and function calling
→ retrieval (RAG)
→ evals, the skill every AI team is hiring for

Resources:
→ Anthropic's free courses on GitHub
→ Hamel Husain's writing on evals

Build:
→ an agent that uses tools and answers from your own documents
→ an eval set that catches when it fails

Checkpoint: you can tell when your agent is wrong before a user does.

MONTH 6: Ship it

Learn:
→ serving models fast and cheap
→ latency, cost and monitoring
→ how to package work so people can use it

Resources:
→ vLLM docs
→ Hugging Face model hub

Build:
→ ONE real project that real people use
→ write up what you built, what broke and what you learned

Checkpoint: a stranger can use your project without asking you how.

The secret nobody tells you:

You don't get hired for finishing courses.

You get hired for the 6 things you BUILT.

Every month ends with a project.

That's your portfolio.

6 months.

$0.

The only cost is consistency.

2113331431254728726.name: The Greatest
2113331431254728726.text:
This is completely f*cking wild.

A Stanford AI researchers gave Claude Code a second brain with JEV. The result? 80+ billion data points processed every 14 minutes.

here's how it works:

Jev stands at the door. every row has to get past it first.

the easy ones it waves through on the spot. only the ones it can't call get sent upstairs to Claude.

the old way:
everything -> Claude -> big bill

the new way:
everything -> Jev -> the tricky few -> Claude

Jev also tells you how sure it is on every call. that number decides who goes upstairs. just don't pick it out of thin air. test it first.

the 20-minute setup:

1. take 200 real rows from your data
2. run them through Jev AND Claude
3. sort Jev's answers by how sure it was
4. find the point where Jev stops disagreeing with Claude. that's your cutoff
5. above it, Jev's answer is final. below it, the row goes to Claude

then do the math. on a public benchmark Jev cost $0.015 per 1,000 rows and Claude cost $0.80.

if Jev settles 80% of your rows:

$0.015 + (20% × $0.80) = $0.175 per 1,000 rows instead of $0.80

that's ~78% off, with Claude still handling every hard case.

3 rules that keep it working:

-> ask all your questions in one Jev call. topic, urgency and sentiment together, not three separate requests
-> once a week, send 50 of Jev's "confident" answers to Claude anyway. if they start disagreeing, raise the cutoff
-> never let Jev make the final call on anything you can't undo. refunds, bans, deletions go to Claude or a human

where this pays off right away:

-> support tickets: route by topic and urgency
-> leads: hot, warm or skip
-> comments: fine, spam or needs a look
-> spreadsheets: fix category labels across thousands of rows

Claude thinks. Jev picks. code ships.

2112887075796111618.name: xsmryze
2112887075796111618.hook: @xsmryze: Anthropic's Claude Code trick - run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each on the job it's best at
2112887075796111618.text:
THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5

2113321574858150261.text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: put a guard between the expensive model and the grunt work. Opus 5.5 asks to read 48 files, the guard says no and hands it to the swarm.

Same session, two ways: all-Opus would have burned $3.41. With the swarm it came out at $0.59. That is $2.82 kept, 83% never burned.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus    # agents: model: haiku

here's the split:
→ Opus 5.5 plans and decides, 97k tokens for $0.52
→ every read, grep and test request gets rerouted to Haiku 5.5
→ 12 Haiku agents map files, find call sites and run tests in parallel
→ Opus comes back to 3 summaries at 6k tokens, never raw files
the part everyone gets wrong: they let the expensive model do the reading.
Opus asked for 48 files in one go. the guard caught it, sent it to the swarm, and that single reroute kept $0.27 on its own.
Haiku is 40x cheaper per token. mapping 32 files, finding 25 call sites, running 212 tests, all of it came in under a cent per lane.

one catch worth knowing: past 100k of context Haiku jumps to 5x its own price, so every agent is kept small on purpose.

grunt work never runs on Opus. that is the whole rule.

Opus thinks. Haiku reads. The guard decides which is which.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 1,420 forks this run - grunt or think, which agent, retry or stop - resolved in code at 0.80 sharpness, and only the split ones ever reach Opus

the full tree
> Opus 5.5 runs the main session, plans and reviews only
> a guard sits between the brain and the tools and reroutes grunt work
> 12 Haiku 5.5 agents fan out across read, grep and test, each kept under 100k
> every agent returns a summary, never raw files or logs
> Opus 5.5 reads 3 summaries at 6k tokens and signs off
> JEV resolves 1,420 micro-forks in code and escalates only the split ones

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Opus 5.5 for planning, decisions and review only.
2. Add a guard: any read, grep or test request from the main session gets rerouted to a Haiku 5.5 agent instead.
3. Fan the grunt work across parallel lanes, each agent kept under 100k of context.
4. Agents return summaries only, raw files and logs never enter the main session.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: grunt work never runs on Opus, no exceptions.

Route deterministic forks (grunt or think, agent choice, retries) through JEV.

Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

holy sh*t, i went to bed and 5 AI agents dug at my question all night

a 6th agent spent the night trying to kill everything they found

9 of 23 findings died before i woke up. the 14 that survived were waiting for me at 07:12, ranked by confidence, with sources

this is not a loop anymore. it is a graph, and the pattern is called the diamond:

-> split: one question becomes 5 angles 
-> gather: 5 researchers dig in parallel, each in its own context window
-> check: a read-only skeptic asks 3 different questions. correct? current? does the source exist? 
-> merge: one writer ranks the survivors 
-> you: the last node. nothing ships without your yes

the part nobody tells you:

a model finds its own error 52.9% of the time. a coin flip. never let an agent grade its own homework

and the stop rule that protects your bill: a graph burns ~15x the tokens. only split work that never reads each other's results

a graph buys breadth, not judgment

2113609423763468306.text:
THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: stop configuring Claude Code by hand. One prompt, 44 seconds, and your whole .claude/ folder writes itself.

7 files, 162 lines, 2 cents. you typed one line and wrote zero of them.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model opus "set up this repo: ..."

here's the split:
→ 3 Haiku 5.5 agents scan the repo before a single file gets written
→ one reads the stack, one reads the npm scripts, one hunts for risky paths
→ Opus 5.5 takes those three summaries and writes the actual config
→ 7 files land: CLAUDE.md, 3 agents, permissions, a format hook and a /ship skill

the part everyone gets wrong: they write CLAUDE.md from memory.

a config written without reading the repo is a guess, and you live with that guess for months.

here the risk scan came back with 5 dangerous paths and those went straight into the permissions file, so the agent is blocked from them before it ever runs once.

the scripts scan found 5 npm scripts, and the agents got wired to the ones that actually exist in this repo instead of generic placeholders.

one prompt from you, 7 files from it, 0 lines written by hand.

Haiku reads. Opus writes. You commit.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 1,867 forks this run - which file, which agent, allow or ask - resolved in code at 0.97 sharpness, and the split ones (0.59 on "allow or ask") come back to you instead of being guessed

the full tree
▸ you paste one prompt describing the setup you want
▸ 3 Haiku 5.5 agents scan stack, scripts and risky paths in parallel
▸ every agent returns a summary, never raw files
▸ Opus 5.5 writes CLAUDE.md, the agents, permissions, the hook and the skill
▸ anything touching permissions comes back to you before it is written
▸ JEV resolves micro-forks in code and escalates only the split ones

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Set up this repo for me:
1. First scan it with 3 Haiku 5.5 agents in parallel: one reads the stack and manifests, one reads the build and npm scripts, one finds paths that are dangerous to touch.
2. Each agent returns a summary only, never raw file contents.
3. Then write CLAUDE.md, 3 subagents, a permissions file, a format hook and a /ship skill, all based on what the scan actually found, not on defaults.
4. Every risky path from the scan goes into the deny list before anything runs.
5. Ask me before writing anything that grants permissions.
Show me every file as a diff first. No writes until I say go."

↳

save it, this is the first thing you run in every new repo.

this harness engineering paper is required reading if you run Claude Code

Wavestone AI Lab read the source code of 11 coding agents, Claude Code and Codex included, and found the same 7-part harness inside every good one

agent = model + harness

the 7 parts, smallest version to largest:
> loop - a plain while loop up to fully replayable runs
> LLM layer - one prompt template up to 29 provider profiles
> tools - bash alone up to 43 typed tools loaded on demand
> memory - raw history up to notes that survive between sessions
> safety - a step limit up to rules, a reviewer model and a sandbox
> orchestration - Aider skips sub-agents, the rest fork them
> extensions - SKILL. md in 9 of the 11, MCP in 8

the pages to open first:
> p.4 - the full 7-part map
> p.12 - three loop types, with Claude Code and Codex as examples
> p.67 - 18 design rules
> p.71 - a 90-line harness that covers all 7 parts

the model gets the headlines
the harness decides whether the agent finishes the job

engineers who can draw these 7 parts on a whiteboard are the ones getting hired to build agents

2113648640661360980.text:
Anthropic cracked open the ribosome and found it stalls on purpose and those pauses are doing a job nobody f*cking gave them

for decades, scientists treated ribosome stalls like a problem.

the machine builds proteins. faster should mean better, right?

turns out, speeding it up might be exactly how you break it.

here’s where things get weird.

researchers used Claude +JEV and started looking at what happens during those tiny pauses instead of just measuring how fast a protein gets made.

> TIME - follow protein production second by second, not just the final result

> MARK - record exactly where the ribosome stops along the sequence

> SORT - separate random slowdowns from pauses that keep appearing in the same places

> FOLD - check what the growing protein is doing during each pause

and that’s when the pattern appeared.

the ribosome wasn’t just randomly getting stuck.

the same pauses kept showing up at the same points, across different cells.

and those points weren’t random either.

they appeared where a newly built section of protein needed time to fold into the right shape.

think about that.

the ribosome isn’t just assembling a chain of amino acids.

it’s giving that chain time to become something that actually works.

remove the pauses and the protein can still come out with every amino acid in the correct order.

except now it folds wrong.

same ingredients. same sequence. completely different result.

and here’s the uncomfortable part.

scientists have spent decades optimizing genes to make proteins faster.

but speeding up the sequence can also erase the pauses that help proteins fold.

we may have been optimizing away part of the instructions.

the genetic code doesn’t just tell the cell what to build.

its timing can also influence how that thing takes shape.

have a look and find some new use cases JEV can do in addition to that

2113718797505036665.name: OpenAI
2113718797505036665.hook: @OpenAI: frontier models now train with no live internet - an offline cached web instead
2113718797505036665.text:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

https://t.co/EmEZsFRMcF

2113571779650224312.name: leopardracer
2113571779650224312.text:
prompt for solar TV:

These are my own solar, battery and home devices on my home network, but I don't know all their brands and models.
If you can't run commands on this computer (you're not Claude Code or a similar agent), say so in one line, tell me to paste this into Claude Code on a computer on my home Wi-Fi, and stop.
Goal: a live full-screen dashboard on my TV that shows my solar power, my house and the weather, and switches screens when I ask out loud.

Find my energy devices. Check my own subnet only (one ping per address; ask me first if it has more than 256 addresses), then the ARP table, mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP). Look for the inverter, battery, smart meter, EV charger, boiler or heat pump and any temperature sensors. For each one, tell me what it is, with brand and model where you can, how sure you are, and how its live data can be read: local API, Modbus TCP, Home Assistant, or the maker's cloud API. If I already run Home Assistant, ask me for it first and use it as the main source.

List what you found and ask what I have that isn't on the network. For anything missing, offer the next best option (a smart plug with metering, a Wi-Fi sensor, the maker's cloud API).
Ask me my city for the weather. Use a free forecast source with no account (Open-Meteo or similar).
Build the dashboard as one local web page plus a small local server, made for a 4K TV seen from the sofa: dark background, big numbers, live updates every few seconds. Three screens:Solar: live power flow between roof, house, battery, grid and boiler, plus today's kWh made, used, sent to the grid and % self-sufficient, battery %, a forecast for the next days, and a year history.
Climate: inside and outside temperature and humidity, plus every room I have a sensor for, with graphs.
Weather: now, the next 24 hours, 14 days, sunrise and sunset, and air quality if it's available.
The screens rotate on their own every 30 seconds and can be switched by URL (/solar, /climate, /weather).

Ask what's plugged into my TV (a smart TV browser, Apple TV, Chromecast, a mini PC over HDMI) and get the dashboard showing full screen on it, opening by itself after a restart.
Voice: ask what I use (Siri, Google, Home Assistant Assist). Set up a phrase like show my solar on my TV that opens the right screen, and a short spoken answer with today's real numbers.
Rules
Only my own devices on my own network. If this computer isn't on my home network (a cloud session, a virtual machine, or WSL without mirrored networking), say so and stop. Never scan or touch any other network.
Read only. Never change a setting on the inverter, battery, charger or meter, even if I ask in passing. If something can only be read by changing a setting, explain it and wait for my yes.
Passwords and tokens never go into the chat. Give me one command to run in my own terminal that saves each one to the system keychain, then read it inside your scripts without printing it.
Keep everything in a solar-tv folder in my home folder, with README.md and CLAUDE.md listing every tool and how to run it, so a new chat in that folder can pick up where you stopped. Keep that folder private and never upload it.

One step at a time. Finish it or tell me it's stuck before moving on, and show me the dashboard in a browser before putting it on the TV.

2113707296492519668.name: mika_systems
2113707296492519668.text:
prompt for Mac:

"Audit this Mac for anything that runs, watches or connects to the internet without me. Read only. Do not delete, disable or change anything

1. Inventory everything that runs on its own: background processes, launch agents and daemons (~/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchDaemons), login items, cron jobs and every browser extension in Chrome, Safari, Arc and Brave. For each one record the publisher, install source, install date and permissions

2. Map the network. For every running process and extension, show which domains and IPs it connects to, how often and at what times (use lsof and nettop). Flag anything that sends data while the Mac is idle, at night or with the lid closed

3. Check trust. Verify code signatures and notarization (codesign, spctl). Flag anything unsigned, installed outside the App Store or the developer's official site, named like a popular app but published by someone else, or talking to a domain registered less than 90 days ago (whois)

4. Review privacy permissions: screen recording, accessibility, input monitoring, full disk access, microphone and camera. List every app that has them and flag the ones I haven't opened in 90 days

5. Search for exposed secrets: API keys, tokens, passwords and seed phrases in plain text across Desktop, Downloads, Documents and shell history. Note which apps and extensions can read my browser profiles and wallet extensions

6. Give me one page ranked by risk: critical, high, low. For each finding show the evidence (path, signature, domain, timestamps), what it can access, the safe fix and what breaks if I apply it. If anything looks active right now, say so first and tell me to change passwords from a different device. Ask before applying any fix"

prompt for Windows:

"Audit this PC for anything that runs, watches or connects to the internet without me. Read only. Do not delete, disable or change anything

1. Inventory everything that runs on its own: Run and RunOnce registry keys (HKCU and HKLM), Startup folders, scheduled tasks, services, WMI event subscriptions and every browser extension in Chrome, Edge, Brave and Firefox. For each one record the publisher, install source, install date and permissions

2. Map the network. For every running process and extension, show which domains and IPs it connects to, how often and at what times (use Get-NetTCPConnection and netstat -abno). Flag anything that sends data while the PC is idle, locked or at night

3. Check trust. Verify digital signatures (Get-AuthenticodeSignature). Flag anything unsigned, installed outside the Microsoft Store or the developer's official site, named like a popular app but published by someone else, or talking to a domain registered less than 90 days ago

4. Review access: apps allowed to use the camera, microphone and location, remote access tools (RDP, AnyDesk, TeamViewer and similar), and any folders or processes excluded from Microsoft Defender scans. Flag anything I haven't opened in 90 days

5. Search for exposed secrets: API keys, tokens, passwords and seed phrases in plain text across Desktop, Downloads, Documents and PowerShell history. Note which apps and extensions can read my browser profiles and wallet extensions

6. Give me one page ranked by risk: critical, high, low. For each finding show the evidence (path, registry key, signature, domain, timestamps), what it can access, the safe fix and what breaks if I apply it. If anything looks active right now, say so first and tell me to change passwords from a different device. Ask before applying any fix"

I asked Claude Code one thing: "what is this Mac doing when I'm not using it?"

6 minutes later it came back with a line I didn't expect:

"a browser extension is sending your open tabs and session cookies to a domain registered 11 days ago"

the extension → a "free PDF converter" with 4.8 stars
the domain → registered 11 days before I installed it
the server → a rented box on a cheap hosting plan
what it had → every URL I opened, plus the session cookie for my exchange
when → every night at 3:12, in one batch

it was still sending while I was reading the report

they never needed my password. the cookie was enough to walk straight in, and 2FA would never get asked

Claude Code told me to log out of every session from my phone first. I did

18 minutes later the exchange sent a login alert from a city I've never been to. the session they tried was already dead

$6,800 in USDC was one transfer away. it's still there

the real PDF tool has millions of users. mine was a copy with a different publisher name and 9 reviews. I installed it from an ad

how not to be me:

→ install extensions from the developer's own site, never from an ad
→ check the publisher name, not just the stars
→ log out of exchanges and banks when you're done. a closed session can't be stolen
→ keep crypto on a hardware wallet, not one browser tab away
→ run a read-only audit once a week

that last one is now a scheduled job. every Sunday night Claude Code checks what runs, what it sends and who signed it, and asks me before touching anything

watch the agents that saved my wallet at work. the full prompts for Mac and Windows are below ↓ free, steal them

2113727094400176464.hook: THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE
2113727094400176464.text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: never let build logs touch your main session. One tiny agent runs the build and hands back 3 lines.

Same build, two ways: inline it is 40k tokens and $0.09 every single run. Through the builder it is 3 lines and nothing.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet    # builder.md: model: haiku

here's the split:
→ Sonnet 5.5 edits code in the main session and never sees a log
→ a Haiku 5.5 builder runs npm build, tsc and the test suite
→ it reads all 2k log lines, 227 files and 18 tests itself
→ it returns 3 lines: what ran, what failed, where

the part everyone gets wrong: they run the build in the main session.

40k tokens of log noise per run, and every later message in that session carries it. you pay for that log again on every turn until the context resets.

the builder agent is 10 lines of markdown. name, model haiku, tools Bash, and one rule: run the build, fix nothing, return 3 lines.

that "fix nothing" is the whole trick. the cheap agent never tries to be clever, it just reports, and the lead decides what to do.

one catch worth knowing: past 100k of context Haiku jumps to 5x its own price, so the builder is kept deliberately small.

main context grows by +0 instead of +40k. that is the entire win.

Sonnet edits. Haiku builds. The log never leaves the agent.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: 1,301 forks this run - which agent, retry or stop, fix or report - resolved in code at 0.90 sharpness, and only the split ones ever reach Sonnet

the full tree
▸ Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code only
▸ a Haiku 5.5 builder agent runs build, typecheck and tests
▸ the builder reads every log line and returns 3 lines, never the log
▸ the builder fixes nothing, it only reports
▸ Sonnet 5.5 reads those 3 lines and decides the next edit
▸ JEV resolves micro-forks in code and escalates only the split ones

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 for editing code only.
2. Create a builder subagent with model: haiku and tools: Bash.
3. The builder runs build, typecheck and tests, reads all output itself, and returns at most 3 lines: what ran, what failed, where.
4. The builder never fixes anything, it only reports.
5. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: build output never enters the main session, no exceptions.
6. Route deterministic forks (which agent, retry or stop, fix or report) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/GoHZ0potb7

save it, it'll come in handy.
